export.law: Export Control Act 2002; Export of Objects of Cultural Interest (Control) Order 2003 (SI 2003/2759); assimilated Regulation (EC) 116/2009 for exports from Northern Ireland. Thresholds unchanged since 2002.

needs.note: Oil or tempera, excluding portraits of British historical personages (those: £10,000).
No separate line; falls under 'any other article over 50 years'.
Under 'any other article'. Hand-produced architectural, scientific or engineering drawings: £0.
Textiles £12,000; arms and armour £35,000; UK archaeological material, manuscripts, documents and archives £0. Objects under 50 years old need no licence.

export.authority: Export Licensing Unit (ELU), Arts Council England, on behalf of the Secretary of State (DCMS). Applications digital, by e-mail; a new online portal has been in development since 2020.
export.fee: The ACE guidance states no fee. Licences are understood to be free of charge (unconfirmed on an official page).
export.time: Not referred: normally 5 business days (object legally imported within the last 50 years). Referred to an Expert Adviser: referral within 5 business days, adviser replies within 15; total normally 28 business days if no objection.
export.temporary: Temporary licence normally for up to 3 years, one extension of up to 3 years; judged on fitness to travel, not national importance. Museums and regular fair exhibitors may hold an OIEL (up to 3 years). ATA carnet is a customs instrument, separate from the licence.
export.treasure: Waverley criteria: history, aesthetics, scholarship; meeting one suffices. The Reviewing Committee (RCEWA) recommends a first deferral of 2–4 months for a serious expression of interest at fair market price, then a second deferral, usually up to 6 months, to complete the sale. Latest year: 5,745 applications, 28,000+ objects, 6 items saved (c. £500,000).
export.eu_licence: Not needed from Great Britain. Northern Ireland: a UK licence for NI to EU; an EU licence (issued by ACE) for NI direct to non-EU countries. UK licences issued before 1 Jan 2021 are not valid for EU exports.
src: gov.uk export licence for cultural goods

import.duty: No customs duty on works of art, collectors' items and antiques (chapter 97 of the UK Global Tariff), whatever the origin (BADA; tariff itself not opened).
import.vat: Import VAT charged at 20% on a reduced valuation, giving an effective 5% (VAT Act 1994 s.21(4)); applies to works of art, collectors' items and antiques over 100 years (headings 97.01–97.06). Standard 20% otherwise.
import.icg: Regulation 2019/880 does not apply in Great Britain. It applies in Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework (ACE page seen in search, not opened).
import.special: Temporary Admission: import VAT suspended against security equal to the 5% VAT or a Customs Comprehensive Guarantee (waiver possible for dealers with a clean record). Chapter 97 commodity codes needed on the declaration; BADA members can issue a certificate of age.
src: BADA, importing from the EU and the rest of the world

apostille.docs: Documents certified by a UK notary or solicitor (powers of attorney, contracts, certified passport copies), court documents with a wet-ink seal, government documents. In an art sale: a notarised provenance affidavit, a notarised bill of sale or authenticity statement for a foreign court or customs; export licences are not usually apostilled.
apostille.authority: FCDO Legalisation Office (get-document-legalised.service.gov.uk).
apostille.fee: £45 standard; £35 e-Apostille; £40 Next-Day (registered businesses); £100 Restricted Urgent (businesses, pre-approved). Plus courier/postage.
apostille.time: Standard up to 25 working days; e-Apostille up to 2 working days; Next-Day next working day; Restricted Urgent same day.

cites.rule: Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing (sale, hire, import/export for sale) in elephant ivory; extended 28 Jan 2025 to hippopotamus, killer whale, narwhal and sperm whale (walrus under separate rules). Exemptions: pre-1918 outstanding items (certificate £250, c. 3 months); pre-1947 items under 10% ivory, pre-1975 instruments under 20%, pre-1918 portrait miniatures (registration £20); museum sales. Max fine £250,000 or 5 years. CITES permits (tortoiseshell, rosewood, coral) via APHA: unconfirmed.
src: gov.uk Declare ivory you intend to sell or hire out (updated 24 Jul 2026)

aml.rule: Money Laundering Regulations 2017 as amended by the 2019 Regulations (in force 10 Jan 2020): 'art market participants' who deal in sales, purchases and storage of works of art worth €10,000 or more (single or linked transactions, any payment method) must register with HMRC and apply customer due diligence (reg 27) on every such transaction.
aml.asks: Identity verification of the buyer, identification of any beneficial owner, and, on a risk basis, source of funds/wealth; records kept. Registration with HMRC (deadline originally 10 Jan 2021).

sanctions.rule: Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019, Schedule 3A (luxury goods, inserted 14 Apr 2022, last amended 20 May 2026): para 21 covers 'works of art, collectors' pieces and antiques, meaning any thing which falls within chapter 97' with no price threshold (other entries carry £250 and higher thresholds). Export, supply to or for use in Russia banned; since 15 Dec 2023 also brokering, financial services and technical assistance. No UK import ban specific to Russian-origin art found.
src: K&L Gates, EU and UK luxury goods sanctions, 8 Aug 2024

export.law: Code du patrimoine, art. L111-1 ff. and R111-1 ff. with Annexe 1 (categories, age and value thresholds); Décret n° 2020-1718 of 28 Dec 2020 raised 11 thresholds from 1 Jan 2021.

needs.note: Other antiquities over 50 years (was €50,000). Archaeology from excavations over 100 years: €0; other archaeology and pre-1500 coins €3,000; post-1500 coins €15,000.

export.authority: Ministère de la Culture, Direction générale des patrimoines et de l'architecture / service des musées de France (export certificates and AST).
export.fee: Not stated on the pages opened; understood to be free (unconfirmed).
export.time: Statutory 4-month decision period (from memory, unconfirmed). Certificate granted automatically to goods imported into France less than 50 years ago; validity unlimited for works over 100 years, 20 years for works aged 50–100 years.
export.temporary: Autorisation de sortie temporaire (AST) for exhibitions, expertise, restoration or deposit in a foreign public collection; AST TN for trésors nationaux (return compulsory). Duration not confirmed. The 2-year re-export window after temporary admission from outside the EU was extended by the 2020 decree.
export.treasure: Refusal of the certificate classifies the work as a trésor national. Within 30 months of refusal the State may make a purchase offer; if the owner declines, experts fix the price; if the State waives acquisition, the work may leave. Advice from the Commission consultative des trésors nationaux.
export.eu_licence: An EU licence (Reg 116/2009) is also needed to leave the EU customs territory, 'désormais nécessaire pour les sorties vers le Royaume-Uni'; EU thresholds unchanged. Archaeology categories 1B/1C exempt from both.
src: Ministère de la Culture, note on certificates and AST, 13 Jan 2021
Ministère de la Culture, circulation des biens culturels

import.duty: 0% (EU common customs tariff, chapter 97; seen for 9705 on a TARIC mirror).
import.vat: 5.5% on imports and intra-EU acquisitions of works of art, collectors' items and antiques (CGI art. 278-0 bis I and 278-0 B). Since 1 Jan 2025 all supplies of works of art are also at 5.5% (loi de finances 2024, art. 83); the dealer's margin-scheme option (art. 297 B) was repealed from 1 Jan 2025. BOFiP text of 14 May 2025 was a consultation draft.
import.icg: Regulation 2019/880 applies in full since 28 June 2025 (licence/statement via the ICG system).
import.special: None found beyond the general EU customs procedures (temporary admission, customs warehousing).

apostille.docs: Actes publics: notarial acts, court decisions, civil-status records, criminal-record extracts. For art: a notarised provenance declaration or power of attorney for use abroad.
apostille.authority: Since 1 May 2025 the notariat (apostille.notaires.fr or the 15 regional notary councils) issues apostilles; legalisations moved to notaries on 1 Sept 2025 (décret n° 2021-1205; arrêté of 10 Apr 2025). Previously the parquets généraux of the 33 cours d'appel.
apostille.fee: Individuals €10 HT per act (first three), €5 from the fourth; legal entities €20/€10; 24-hour express €20 (page footnotes conflict).
apostille.time: No standard time stated; 24-hour express option.
src: Barreau de Paris, L'apostille: ce qui change (updated 2 Jul 2025)

cites.rule: EU regime applies (Reg 338/97; ivory rules in force 19 Jan 2022: no commercial import/export permits, intra-EU sale of worked ivory only with a certificate proving pre-1947 manufacture). See EU entry.
src: BADA on EU ivory rules from 19 Jan 2022

aml.rule: AMLD5 transposed: art dealers and intermediaries (and freeport operators) are obliged entities for transactions of €10,000 or more (Code monétaire et financier, not opened). From 10 July 2027 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 applies directly (see EU).
aml.asks: ID, beneficial owner, source of funds on a risk basis (generic; French guidance not opened).
src: NRW tax administration note on EU AML Regulation obliged entities

sanctions.rule: EU Regulation 833/2014 applies directly (Art 3h luxury goods incl. art over €300 per item; Art 5b deposits over €100,000). See EU entry.

export.law: Kulturgutschutzgesetz (KGSG) of 31 July 2016, § 24: exports to third countries need a licence under Reg 116/2009; exports to other EU states need a licence above national age and value thresholds (not for works owned by their creator).

needs.note: Intra-EU threshold (§ 24(2) Nr 3). To third countries: Reg 116/2009 (50 years, €150,000).
Drawings and mosaics (Nr 5) €50,000; watercolours, gouaches, pastels (Nr 4) €100,000.
Nr 15 other antiques 100 years/€100,000; archives Nr 12 50 years/€50,000; means of transport 150 years/€100,000; otherwise Reg 116/2009 ages with double the EU values.

export.authority: Oberste Landesbehörde für Kultur of the Land where the object is located when the application is filed (§ 24(6)).
export.fee: Set by Land law; not stated in § 24 (unconfirmed).
export.time: Decision within 10 working days of a complete application (§ 24(7)). Value = price paid within the last 3 years, otherwise a reasoned domestic estimate (§ 24(4)).
export.temporary: Objects proven to be in Germany only temporarily (up to 2 years) are exempt from the intra-EU licence (§ 24(8)); temporary export licences and general open licences for museums under § 22 (not opened).
export.treasure: 'National wertvolles Kulturgut' entered in a Land register (§§ 7–14 KGSG) may not be exported without permission; licence must be granted if no export ban under § 21 applies (§ 24(5)). Register mechanism not opened.
export.eu_licence: Needed for any export to a non-EU country (§ 24(1) Nr 1 refers to Reg 116/2009); national thresholds only govern intra-EU movements.

import.duty: 0% (EU chapter 97).
import.vat: 7% on imports, intra-EU acquisitions and supplies of works of art (§ 12(2) Nr 1 UStG with Anlage 2 Nr 53). The Jahressteuergesetz 2024 restored the reduced rate for all supplies from 1 Jan 2025 and repealed § 12(2) Nr 12 and 13 UStG.
import.icg: Regulation 2019/880 applies since 28 June 2025; German competent authority information at kunstverwaltung.bund.de (not opened).
src: Bayerisches Landesamt für Steuern, Verfügung 14 Jan 2025 (S 7220.2.1-33/111)

apostille.docs: Notarial deeds and court documents (apostilled by the Landgericht president of the district), administrative documents (Land interior authorities), federal documents (Bundesverwaltungsamt). Authorities vary by Land; the AA page names none.
apostille.authority: Varies: Bundesverwaltungsamt for federal documents; Land justice and interior authorities otherwise (allocation from memory).
apostille.fee: Fee-based ('gebührenpflichtige Amtshandlung'); amounts vary by Land, typically around €25 (unconfirmed).
apostille.time: No fixed time; the Federal Foreign Office warns of long waits ('lange Wartezeiten').
src: Auswärtiges Amt FAQ on the Hague apostille

cites.rule: EU regime applies (Reg 338/97; ivory rules from 19 Jan 2022). See EU entry.

aml.rule: Geldwäschegesetz: Güterhändler, Kunstvermittler and Kunstlagerhalter are obliged entities from €10,000 (cash and non-cash). From 10 July 2027 Reg 2024/1624 Art 3(3)(i),(j) applies: traders and intermediaries in cultural goods (galleries, auction houses) and storers in free zones/customs warehouses, €10,000; 'cultural goods' follow Annex I of Reg 116/2009.
aml.asks: Identification of the customer and beneficial owner, purpose of the transaction, source of funds on a risk basis (NRW page does not detail).

sanctions.rule: EU Regulation 833/2014 applies directly. See EU entry.

export.law: Codice dei beni culturali e del paesaggio (D.Lgs. 42/2004), art. 65 and 68, as amended by L. 124/2017 and by Legge 17 marzo 2026 n. 40 (GU 30 Mar 2026): the value threshold for works by deceased authors made over 70 years ago rose from €13,500 to €50,000.

needs.note: Author deceased, made over 70 years ago, value above €50,000: attestato di libera circolazione (art. 68). Below €50,000 or under 70 years/living author: self-declaration (DPR 445/2000) to the Ufficio Esportazione.

Books and library goods keep the €13,500 threshold; private archives and documents of cultural interest and art. 11(1)(f),(g),(h) categories need authorisation at any value. Vincolati beni culturali (art. 10) may never leave definitively.

export.authority: Uffici Esportazione of the Ministero della Cultura (Soprintendenze), via the SUE online portal (from memory, unconfirmed).
export.fee: No fee found; stamp duty on the application likely (unconfirmed).
export.time: Decision period for the attestato (40 days in the Code, from memory) not confirmed; L. 40/2026 sets 90 days for loan authorisations. The applicant may withdraw the request before the final decision. Self-declaration validity now aligned with the attestato's duration (art. 65(4-ter)).
export.temporary: Attestato di circolazione temporanea (art. 71) for exhibitions and fairs (not opened; unconfirmed).
export.treasure: Dichiarazione dell'interesse culturale (notifica/vincolo, art. 13) makes a work inexportable; a temporary ban applies to works by deceased authors over 70 years until the verification under art. 12. Under L. 40/2026 the attestato cannot be refused to works by foreign authors unless specific relevance to Italian cultural history is established. Constitutional Court judgment 51/2026 on sub-€13,500 works not opened.
export.eu_licence: EU licence (Reg 116/2009) also required for exports outside the EU above the EU thresholds (standard EU rule; Italian page not opened).
src: Art. 65 Codice dei beni culturali (Brocardi, consolidated with L. 40/2026)

import.duty: 0% (EU chapter 97).
import.vat: 5% on imports and sales of works of art, antiques and collectors' items from 1 July 2025 (decreto-legge 30 June 2025 n. 95); previously 10% on imports and 22% on dealer sales (prior rates from memory). Margin scheme restricted for goods bought or imported at 5%.

apostille.docs: Notarial and judicial documents via the Procura della Repubblica; administrative documents via the Prefettura (from memory).
apostille.authority: Procura della Repubblica / Prefettura (unconfirmed).

cites.rule: EU regime applies. See EU entry.

aml.rule: AMLD5 transposed (D.Lgs. 231/2007 as amended by D.Lgs. 125/2019): art dealers, intermediaries and freeport operators obliged from €10,000 (not opened). Reg 2024/1624 applies from 10 July 2027.
aml.asks: ID, beneficial owner, source of funds (generic).

sanctions.rule: EU Regulation 833/2014 applies directly. See EU entry.

export.law: Erfgoedwet (Heritage Act, in force 1 July 2016), art. 4.23: protected cultural goods (beschermde cultuurgoederen, listed in the register) may not leave the Netherlands without permission; Reg 116/2009 for exports outside the EU.

needs.note: No national thresholds for unlisted works; EU licence above the Reg 116/2009 thresholds when leaving the EU. Listed (protected) objects need permission for any destination.

export.authority: Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed, in cooperation with the Belastingdienst/Douane; apply to Customs for an 'uitvoervergunning cultuurgoederen'. Export by post or courier not permitted.
export.temporary: Temporary export licences exist under the EU regulation; Dutch details not opened.
export.treasure: Register of protected cultural goods under the Erfgoedwet; export of listed objects requires ministerial permission (government.nl refers to art. 4.23 Erfgoedwet).
export.eu_licence: Needed for exports outside the EU above the Reg 116/2009 thresholds.
src: government.nl, applying for an export licence for cultural goods

import.duty: 0% (EU chapter 97).
import.vat: 9% reduced rate retained for culture, media and sport from 1 Jan 2026 (Wet van 29 Oct 2025, Stb. 2025, 339, reversing the planned rise to 21%; only accommodation goes to 21%). Imports of works of art fall under the 9% rate (Tabel I; Dutch tax page not opened).

apostille.docs: Notarial and court documents apostilled by the rechtbank (district court); fee about €25 (from memory).
apostille.authority: Rechtbanken (unconfirmed).

cites.rule: EU regime applies. See EU entry.

aml.rule: Wwft: art dealers and intermediaries obliged from €10,000 (AMLD5 transposition; not opened). Reg 2024/1624 applies from 10 July 2027.
aml.asks: ID, beneficial owner, source of funds (generic).

sanctions.rule: EU Regulation 833/2014 applies directly. See EU entry.

export.law: Ley 16/1985 del Patrimonio Histórico Español (arts. 5, 29–33) and Real Decreto 111/1986 (arts. 45–51): export permit for goods over 100 years old and goods in the Inventario General; BIC inexportable (art. 5 not opened).

needs.note: Any value if over 100 years old or inventoried; plus EU licence above Reg 116/2009 thresholds when leaving the EU.

Works by living authors exempt from the export tax; goods legally imported within the last 10 years may be exported under licence without pre-emption and cannot be declared BIC for 10 years (art. 32).

export.authority: Ministerio de Cultura (Dirección General de Bellas Artes), or the Comunidad Autónoma where it has taken over processing, after the opinion of the Junta de Calificación, Valoración y Exportación (RD 111/1986 arts. 47–48).
export.fee: Export tax (art. 30 LPHE) on definitive exports: 5% up to 1,000,000 pesetas; 10% to 10,000,000; 20% to 100,000,000; 30% above (euro equivalents c. €6,010 / €60,101 / €601,012, own conversion). Exempt: goods imported within 10 years, temporary exports, works by living authors.
export.time: Decision within 3 months of receipt; silence may be taken as approval, with a certification issued within 20 days of request (RD 111/1986 art. 49).
export.temporary: Temporary export permit (art. 31): the authorisation fixes the term and guarantees; not subject to the State's pre-emptive purchase; failure to return is treated as illegal export.
export.treasure: The declared value in a definitive export request is an irrevocable offer of sale to the State; on refusal the State has 6 months to accept and 1 year to pay (art. 33 LPHE; RD art. 50). The Ministry may declare an item inexportable as a precaution while a protection file is opened (RD art. 51).
export.eu_licence: Needed for exports outside the EU above the Reg 116/2009 thresholds, in addition to the national permit.

import.duty: 0% (EU chapter 97).
import.vat: 10% on imports of works of art, antiques and collectors' items whoever the importer (art. 91.Uno.4 Ley 37/1992); 10% on sales by the artist or heirs; 21% general rate otherwise; dealers use the margin scheme (REBU, arts. 135–139). Spain had not transposed Directive 2022/542 as of Feb 2026.
src: Cuatrecasas, El tipo impositivo del IVA en el mercado del arte español (6 Feb 2026)

apostille.docs: Notarial documents apostilled by the Colegios Notariales; judicial and administrative documents by the Ministerio de Justicia (from memory).
apostille.authority: Ministerio de Justicia / Colegios Notariales (unconfirmed).

cites.rule: EU regime applies. See EU entry.

aml.rule: Ley 10/2010: art dealers and intermediaries obliged from €10,000 (AMLD5 transposition; not opened). Reg 2024/1624 applies from 10 July 2027.
aml.asks: ID, beneficial owner, source of funds (generic).

sanctions.rule: EU Regulation 833/2014 applies directly. See EU entry.

export.law: Bundesgesetz über den internationalen Kulturgütertransfer (KGTG, SR 444.1, in force 1 June 2005) and Verordnung KGTV (SR 444.11); customs directive BAZG R-60-2.7 (valid from 1 Jan 2026). No general export licence.

needs.note: No licence; every cultural good must be declared at export with object type, place of manufacture or find, dating and dimensions.
Only objects in the federal register (state-owned) need a BAK permit for temporary export; their permanent export is prohibited. Cantonal restrictions may apply.

export.authority: Bundesamt für Kultur (BAK), Fachstelle Internationaler Kulturgütertransfer, for register objects; cantons for cantonal registers; BAZG (customs) for declarations.
export.temporary: Temporary admission (ZAVV declaration or ATA carnet) for exhibitions, sales exhibitions and auctions; durations not stated on the page.
export.treasure: Federal register (Bundesverzeichnis) of federal cultural property: permanent export prohibited; cantonal registers under cantonal law. Unlawful export only where the good was imported in breach of a bilateral agreement (Art. 7 KGTG) or is a listed state object (Art. 24(1)(d)).
export.eu_licence: Not applicable (non-EU). Entering the EU, Swiss-held works need a Reg 2019/880 licence or statement; Switzerland is relevant for works held there over 5 years when the country of origin cannot be reliably determined.
src: BAK, Informationen und FAQ zum Kunsthandel und Auktionswesen
Borel & Barbey art law newsletter, Sept 2025

import.duty: Works of art for long-term public display may be imported duty-free on an undertaking not to sell (form 11.32); artists' own works duty-free. General abolition of industrial tariffs from 1 Jan 2024 (not opened). Handcrafts are not works of art.
import.vat: Import VAT at the standard rate of 8.1% (since 1 Jan 2024); no reduced rate for art (rate page not opened). Dealers may use the VAT transfer procedure (Verlagerungsverfahren) for art imports (unconfirmed).
import.icg: Not applicable; the BAK fact sheet (11 Jul 2025) explains the EU rules for goods leaving Switzerland.
import.special: Imports from states with a bilateral agreement (Art. 7 KGTG) need proof of lawful export recorded in the declaration. Storage in a customs warehouse counts as an import under the KGTG: written notice to BAZG on form 11.95 in duplicate.
src: BAZG, works of art and exhibition objects
BAK fact sheet on EU Reg 2019/880 (11 Jul 2025)

apostille.docs: Cantonal documents (notarial deeds, court documents) apostilled by the cantonal chancellery; federal documents by the Federal Chancellery (from memory).
apostille.authority: Cantonal Staatskanzlei / Federal Chancellery (unconfirmed).

cites.rule: Swiss CITES rules (Federal Act on Trade in Protected Species) apply; ivory and other Annex A items need permits; not opened.

aml.rule: Art dealers are not financial intermediaries under the AMLA; cash sales above CHF 100,000 trigger AML duties for traders (from memory). KGTG Art. 16 due diligence: identify the seller (name, date of birth, address, nationality), obtain a written declaration of the right to dispose, inform clients of import/export rules, keep records 30 years; exempt below CHF 5,000 except archaeology, palaeontology, ethnology and monument fragments.
aml.threshold: CHF 5,000 (KGTG due diligence); CHF 100,000 cash (AMLA, unconfirmed)
aml.asks: Seller identity and written declaration of right to dispose; buyer identity for cash above CHF 100,000.
src: BAK, Informationen und FAQ zum Kunsthandel und Auktionswesen

sanctions.rule: Switzerland has aligned with the EU luxury goods ban (Ordinance on measures in connection with the situation in Ukraine), including works of art over CHF 300 per item (from memory; SECO page not opened).

freeport.rule: Geneva Ports Francs: Swiss Federal Audit Office found 245 open customs warehouses (2012) and 10 free ports (2013, down from 18 in 2008); goods in 201 warehouses over CHF 15bn, suspended duties over CHF 1bn; press figure of CHF 100bn in Geneva unverified; 841 free-port controls in 2012; 8 recommendations. Storage counts as import under the KGTG (form 11.95; stock-record entry compulsory). 2016 inventory rules, storage fees and the new customs law not confirmed.
src: EFK/CDF audit summary of customs warehouses and free ports

eu.n: European Union (applies to FR, DE, IT, NL, ES)

export.law: Council Regulation (EC) No 116/2009 on the export of cultural goods (codified); Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1081/2012. A licence is needed to export listed goods outside the EU customs territory; it is issued by the Member State where the object is lawfully and definitively located (Art 2(2)).

needs.note: A.3: pictures and paintings executed entirely by hand, over 50 years old and not belonging to their originators.
A.7: original sculptures or statuary and copies by the same process.
A.5 drawings and hand-executed mosaics €15,000; A.4 watercolours, gouaches, pastels €30,000.
A.6: original engravings, prints, serigraphs, lithographs, posters.

A.15 other antiques 50–100 years (listed types) or over 100 years; archaeology and monument parts over 100 years, manuscripts, archives over 50 years: whatever the value; books over 100 years €50,000; maps over 200 years €15,000.

export.authority: Competent authority of the Member State (e.g. ministries of culture); value assessed at the date of application.
export.temporary: Temporary and open licences exist under the implementing regulation (not opened).
export.treasure: National 'treasure' regimes sit alongside: a national licence may be refused even where the EU licence would be due.
export.eu_licence: The EU licence only governs exit from the EU customs territory; movements between Member States are governed by national rules (e.g. DE, FR, IT thresholds).

import.duty: 0% erga omnes on chapter 97 (seen for 9705 10 00 on a TARIC mirror).
import.vat: Rates national (FR 5.5%, DE 7%, IT 5%, NL 9%, ES 10%); Directive 2022/542 allows reduced rates on art supplies but bars combining them with the margin scheme.
import.icg: Regulation (EU) 2019/880 applies since 28 June 2025. Part B (import licence): archaeological objects and dismembered parts of monuments over 250 years old, any value. Part C (importer statement): other listed goods over 200 years old and worth over €18,000 per item. Both filed in the central ICG system (EU CSW-CERTEX). 'Import' includes free circulation, customs warehousing, free zones, temporary admission, end-use and inward processing. Exemptions: returned goods; educational/scientific use. Licence decisions within 90 days.
import.special: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/1079 sets formats and exemptions. Works created in the EU are outside the scope (recital; not opened). A document declared under the wrong customs procedure causes rejection.
src: European Commission Access2Markets, new import controls on cultural goods
BAK fact sheet on Reg 2019/880 (11 Jul 2025)

apostille.docs: All eight jurisdictions are parties to the Hague Apostille Convention (1961); competent authorities are national. Within the EU, Regulation 2016/1191 exempts certain public documents (civil status, company extracts) from apostille between Member States (from memory).
apostille.authority: National.

cites.rule: Regulation (EC) 338/97 (wildlife trade). Ivory: from 19 Jan 2022 (Commission Reg 2021/2280 and revised guidance) Member States should not issue import permits or re-export certificates for ivory for commercial purposes, except pre-1947 items sold to museums and pre-1975 musical instruments; intra-EU sale of worked ivory only with a commercial certificate proving manufacture before 1947; no percentage de minimis. Tortoiseshell, rosewood (Dalbergia, Annex B) and coral: permit regime not opened.
src: BADA, EU ivory rules from 19 Jan 2022

aml.rule: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), applying from 10 July 2027: obliged entities include persons trading in or intermediating cultural goods (galleries, auction houses) and persons storing, trading or intermediating cultural goods and other high-value goods in free zones and customs warehouses, for transactions of at least €10,000 (Art 3(3)(i),(j)); 'cultural goods' = Annex I of Reg 116/2009. EU-wide cash limit €10,000; occasional-transaction CDD at €10,000 (€3,000 cash). AMLA (Frankfurt) supervises from 2025/2028 (not opened). Until then AMLD5 national rules apply.
aml.asks: Customer identification and verification, beneficial owner (25% rule, from memory), purpose of the business relationship, source of funds on a risk basis.
src: NRW Finanzverwaltung note on Reg 2024/1624 obliged entities

sanctions.rule: Regulation 833/2014 Art 3h: ban on selling, supplying, transferring or exporting Annex XVIII luxury goods (incl. works of art, chapter 97) to any person in Russia or for use in Russia, where the value exceeds €300 per item unless otherwise specified; since Dec 2023 regardless of origin; brokering and financing also banned. Belarus: similar restriction since June 2024. Art 5b: no deposits over €100,000 per credit institution from Russian nationals/residents or Russian entities (EU/EEA/Swiss nationals and residence-permit holders excepted). No EU import ban specific to Russian-origin art found.
src: K&L Gates, EU and UK luxury goods sanctions, 8 Aug 2024

freeport.rule: Reg 2024/1624 brings operators storing or trading cultural and high-value goods in free zones and customs warehouses within AML duties from 10 July 2027; AMLD5 already covers freeport operators (UK and EU transpositions). Luxembourg's Le Freeport (Findel): press titles seen suggest conversion to a 'Luxembourg High Security Hub' / defence depot, but no page could be opened; status in 2026 unconfirmed.

items.figure: Condition baseline (images, measurements), crate/packing selection incl. climate lining, route planning with custody checkpoints, all-risk insurance at declared value, export/import documentation and brokerage, delivery, acclimation and unpacking. Shippers price on dimensions, weight, destination, pick-up/delivery, mode, timeframe and extras.

Fine Art Shippers, NYC to Europe

International airfreight airport-to-airport, crated, with broker $900–2,200; white-glove door-to-door international with brokerage $1,800–4,500; local art shuttle $250–650; domestic road door-to-door crated $600–1,500. No Europe–New York or intra-Europe figure for a 100×100 cm painting was published: U.
All-risk 0.15%–0.45% of declared value per leg, minimum premium $150–300. Annual fine-art policy rates (per cent of value per year): no published figure opened: U.
Entry and clearance fees $120–450 per shipment; temporary import bonds 0.5%–1.5% of value pro-rated plus admin fees (US-style figures). UK/EU broker tariffs: U.
Two-person crew with hardware $250–900 depending on site.

law_world.method: Primary sources opened where possible (HCCH status table, Senate PSI report, CFR mirror checked 3 Nov 2026, State Dept, FWS, HK Customs and Government, Singapore Customs, Abu Dhabi Culture, Office for the Arts, Agency for Cultural Affairs, NY Tax Dept, Bank of Slovenia). vf: V = read on a primary source; S = secondary (law firm, trade press, broker); U = carried from memory or a weak page, see note.

export.law: No export licence for works of art as such. Export rules touch art only through CITES/ESA (ivory, tortoiseshell), OFAC sanctions programmes and the EAR luxury-goods rule for Russia and Belarus (15 CFR 746 Supp. 5). No federal cultural-property export control exists.
export.needs: Nothing for a painting, sculpture or work on paper beyond the shipper’s routine export declaration. An FWS declaration is needed if the object contains CITES-listed material. Nothing opened this session states the negative on an official page; the absence is inferred from the sources read.
export.authority: None for art. US Fish and Wildlife Service for ESA/CITES species; BIS and OFAC for sanctions.
export.temporary: The US accepts ATA carnets (issued in the US by the US Council for International Business); works brought in on temporary entry that sell at a US fair become dutiable on re-import (Cultural Property News, Nov 2025).
src: Cultural Property News, The New Costs of Collecting, 7 Nov 2025
FWS, What can I do with my ivory
export.note: Carnet acceptance carried from memory (U); no official CBP carnet page opened.

import.duty: HTSUS chapter 97 (9701 paintings, 9702 original prints, 9703 sculpture, 9705 collectors’ pieces, 9706 antiques over 100 years) is ‘Free’ at the MFN rate in the 2026 schedule.
import.overlays: IEEPA ‘reciprocal’ and fentanyl tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court on 20 Feb 2026 (Learning Resources v. Trump); art had anyway been treated as exempt ‘informational materials’ (50 USC 1702(b)(3)). A s.122 surcharge (10%, then 15%) ran 24 Feb–24 Jul 2026 with the same exemption. The s.301 forced-labour tariffs from 24 Jul 2026 (10–12.5%, c.60–80 economies) exclude all of chapter 97 (HTSUS 9903.05.86; 91 FR 47318).
import.overlays_note: Chinese-origin art still bears the 7.5% s.301 List 4A duty (15% from Sept 2019, halved in 2020; The Art Newspaper, Dec 2023; not re-checked on USTR this session). Canadian-origin art is reported to fall under separate 2026 Canada tariffs (The Art Newspaper, 28 Jul 2026; rate unconfirmed). IEEPA refunds run through CBP’s CAPE process (c.US$165bn). The US$800 de minimis exemption is gone, so every shipment is formally entered.
import.vat: No federal VAT. State sales or use tax attaches where the work is delivered or first used.
import.state_tax: New York: use tax (NYC 8.875%) on art bought elsewhere and used in NY, but property bought while a non-resident is exempt (Tax Law §1118(2); TSB-A-08(7)S, 14 Feb 2008); carrying on business in NY makes one a resident. Delaware has no sales tax. California and Florida use-tax rules, and NY’s 2017 six-month amendment, were not opened this session (U).
import.cpia: Under the Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act the US restricts import of archaeological/ethnological material from 32 countries (State Dept Cultural Heritage Center list, archived to May 2025) plus Nepal from 12 Aug 2026 (CBP Dec. 26-16, to 8 Jan 2031); modern paintings and sculpture are not covered.
src: DLA Piper, Supreme Court holds IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, 24 Feb 2026
Sullivan & Worcester via JD Supra, art after the IEEPA decision, 4 Mar 2026
The Art Newspaper, new tariffs largely exempt art and antiques, 28 Jul 2026
Cultural Property News, chapter 97 excluded from the 2026 s.301 action (91 FR 47318), 4 Aug 2026
The Art Newspaper, tariffs on art and China–US relations, 26 Dec 2023
Artnet, what the US–China deal means for art tariffs
NY Dept of Taxation and Finance, TSB-A-08(7)S
State Dept ECA (archive 2012–2025), current agreements and import restrictions
Federal Register public inspection, CBP Dec. 26-16, Nepal import restrictions, 12 Aug 2026
import.note: Tariff overlays rest on trade press and law-firm notes that cite the Federal Register (91 FR 47318, 28 Jul 2026); the FR notice itself was not opened. CPIA list and Nepal rule read on official pages (V).

apostille.docs: Notarised provenance affidavits, powers of attorney for a consignment and corporate certificates are apostilled by the Secretary of State of the state that commissioned the notary; only federal documents go to the State Department (split carried from memory, U). Customs itself does not require apostilles.
apostille.authority: Office of Authentications, US Department of State (600 19th St NW, Washington DC; Form DS-4194) for federal documents; state Secretaries of State for notarised documents. Party since 15 Oct 1981 (accession 24 Dec 1980).
apostille.fee: US$20 per document (federal office; non-refundable). State fees vary.
apostille.time: Mail-in: up to 5 weeks from receipt. Walk-in: 7 business days (drop-off Mon–Thu 7:30–9:00). Same-day only for family emergencies abroad.
src: State Dept Office of Authentications, request services

cites.rule: FWS Division of Management Authority issues CITES permits; all wildlife imports/exports are declared to FWS Law Enforcement. African elephant ivory 4(d) rule in force 6 Jul 2016: commercial import banned; ESA antiques (100+ years, unmodified since 1973, entered via an antique port) may move with CITES papers; interstate sale only for ESA antiques or de minimis items (<200 g, <50% of value, pre-2016); raw ivory may not be exported. NY and CA laws are stricter (U).
src: FWS, What can I do with my ivory

aml.rule: Art dealers and auction houses are not BSA ‘financial institutions’. The AML Act 2020 added antiquities dealers and ordered a Treasury study of art (no rule for either). The Art Market Integrity Act (Grassley, Whitehouse, Fetterman, Cassidy, Kim, McCormick; announced 23–29 Jul 2025) would add ‘a person engaged in the trade in works of art’ with full BSA duties. As of 3 Nov 2026 no enactment or FinCEN art rule was found.
aml.threshold: Bill: exempt if no single art transaction above US$10,000 or under US$50,000 of art transactions in the prior year; artists selling their own work exempt. Current law: cash over US$10,000 is reported on Form 8300 by any trade (U).
aml.asks: Houses ask for government ID, proof of address, a beneficial-owner declaration and, above internal thresholds, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth papers; the 2020 PSI report found all four houses treated the agent as principal and did not ask for whom he bought, which they have since changed (practice, not opened on a house page this session).
src: DLA Piper, Art Market Integrity Act introduced, 21 Aug 2025
Senate PSI staff report, The Art Industry and U.S. Policies that Undermine Sanctions, 29 Jul 2020
aml.note: Bill status after Aug 2025 not found in a 2026 source; treated as pending. House KYC practice is U.

sanctions.rule: OFAC SDN screening and the 50% rule apply to every sale. EAR 15 CFR 746 Supp. 5 (per §746.8(a)(7); §746.10 is now reserved): paintings, prints, sculpture, collectors’ pieces and antiques with a US wholesale value of US$300 or more per unit are ‘luxury goods’ barred for export or re-export to Russia or Belarus, and to listed oligarchs wherever located. No US ban on importing Russian-origin art was found; EO 14068’s import bans cover fish, seafood, alcohol and diamonds (U).
sanctions.detail: FinCEN alert of 16 Mar 2022 (number FIN-2022-Alert003 not shown on the page opened) names artworks among high-value assets used to evade Russia sanctions and lists red flags (shell companies, parties linked to sanctioned Russians, art-insurance changes). Senate PSI report of 29 Jul 2020 traced over US$18m of 2014 art purchases to Rotenberg-linked shell companies via Christie’s, Sotheby’s and private sales after their 20 Mar 2014 designation.
src: 15 CFR 746 Supplement No. 5 (regulation mirror, checked 3 Nov 2026)
Covington, FinCEN alert on evasion of Russia sanctions, 17 Mar 2022
sanctions.note: Supplement 5 read on a CFR mirror, not ecfr.gov (refused). EO 14068 import-ban list from memory.

freeport.rule: Delaware Freeport (Newark, DE; conceived by Fritz Dietl; opened Sept 2015; 36,000 sq ft) stores art in a state with no sales tax, two hours from New York, where a buyer would pay 8.875%. Chapter 97 is duty-free, so US bonded warehouses and the JFK/Newark foreign-trade zones matter for state use tax and deferral only; use tax attaches when the work enters the owner’s home state. ARCIS (Harlem) and NY bonded storage not opened (U). Fees not published.
src: NY Dept of Taxation and Finance, TSB-A-08(7)S (art stored in Delaware)

jurisdictions.n: United Arab Emirates (Dubai and Abu Dhabi)

export.law: No export licence for works of art. Antiquities fall under Federal Law 11 of 2017 on antiquities and emirate heritage rules (Dubai Culture, Abu Dhabi DCT) — carried from memory.
export.needs: Nothing for a painting or sculpture beyond the customs exit declaration; antiquities need the heritage authority’s consent (U).
export.authority: Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs and Port Security; Dubai Customs; Abu Dhabi Customs. Abu Dhabi’s waiver committee must approve temporary export of works admitted under the duty-waiver programme.
export.temporary: ATA carnets are accepted (Dubai Chamber is the national guaranteeing body) — from memory (U).
src: Abu Dhabi Culture, Art Customs Duty Waiver Programme
export.note: No official UAE page on art export opened; only the Abu Dhabi waiver page (which refers to an export licence or shipping information as a document to supply).

import.duty: 5% GCC common customs duty on works of art at first point of entry (rate from memory; not confirmed on an official page this session). Abu Dhabi’s Art Customs Duty Waiver Programme (live in 2026; reported launched Jan 2026) waives the duty for individual applicants’ artworks independently appraised at AED 10 million or more, on condition the work stays in Abu Dhabi at least three years; provenance, ownership history and due-diligence papers are mandatory.
import.overlays: Goods held in a free zone (JAFZA, DAFZ, DMCC) stay duty-suspended until they enter the mainland (U).
import.vat: 5% VAT charged on import at the customs value plus duty (rate from memory, U).
src: Abu Dhabi Culture, Art Customs Duty Waiver Programme
import.note: Waiver conditions read on the official page (V); the 5% duty and 5% VAT rates are U this session.

apostille.docs: Foreign public documents for use in the UAE (notarised provenance affidavits, powers of attorney, corporate papers) need the full legalisation chain: notary, home-state authentication, UAE embassy legalisation, then attestation by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs (chain from memory, U).
apostille.authority: UAE embassies abroad and the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs (attestation).
apostille.fee: Not established (MOFA attestation fee from memory c.AED 150 per document, U).
src: HCCH status table, Apostille Convention (UAE absent)
apostille.note: The UAE does not appear in the HCCH status table as of 3 Nov 2026, so it is not a party; the legalisation chain itself is U.

cites.rule: Ministry of Climate Change and Environment is the CITES management authority under Federal Law 11 of 2002; ivory and other Appendix I material need CITES permits on each movement — from memory (U).

aml.rule: Federal Decree-Law 10 of 2025 (in force 14 Oct 2025) replaced the 2018 AML law; Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025 (14 Dec 2025) replaced Cabinet Decision 10 of 2019. DNFBPs that must register on goAML: real-estate brokers, auditors/accountants, corporate and trust service providers, lawyers and notaries, dealers in precious metals and stones, gaming operators, VASPs. Art dealers, galleries and auction houses are not named as DNFBPs.
aml.threshold: AED 55,000 cash for dealers in precious metals and stones (DPMS report). Art has no statutory threshold.
aml.asks: Dubai and Abu Dhabi auction houses and fairs apply group KYC (ID, address, beneficial owner, source of funds) voluntarily or under free-zone (DIFC/ADGM) rules — practice, U.

sanctions.rule: The UAE applies UN sanctions only and has adopted no Russia sanctions (U). FATF grey-listed the UAE in 2022 and removed it on 23 Feb 2024 after reforms (The National: Dh1.3bn/US$354m of assets seized Mar–Jul 2023; Dh199m fines in a half-year). ‘Dubai Unlocked’ (14 May 2024; C4ADS data via OCCRP/E24) mapped over 1,000 Dubai properties held by 200 flagged owners; a sourced total for Russian-owned Dubai property was not found this session.
src: The National, UAE removed from FATF grey list, 23 Feb 2024

freeport.rule: Dubai’s free zones (DMCC, Dubai Airport Free Zone, JAFZA) offer duty-suspended storage and licences for art trading companies; no purpose-built art freeport comparable to Geneva was confirmed this session. Abu Dhabi’s waiver programme instead ties the duty relief to the work staying in the emirate for three years.
src: Abu Dhabi Culture, Art Customs Duty Waiver Programme

export.law: No export licence for works of art. The Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (Cap. 53) covers antiquities and monuments in Hong Kong, not the trade in imported art (U). Import and export declarations must be lodged with Customs within 14 days of shipment under the Import and Export (Registration) Regulations (U).
export.needs: Nothing for a painting, sculpture or work on paper; a CITES licence from AFCD if the object contains listed species.
export.authority: Customs and Excise Department (declarations); AFCD (CITES).
export.fee: Declaration charge of HK$0.20 per HK$1,000 of value (U).
export.temporary: ATA carnets accepted (Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce issues) — U.
export.note: No official Hong Kong page on art export or declaration opened this session.

import.duty: None. Hong Kong is a free port: no customs duty on art; only liquor, tobacco, hydrocarbon oil and methyl alcohol are dutiable (U).
import.overlays: None.
import.vat: No VAT, GST or sales tax.
import.note: Well-established position but not confirmed on an official page this session.

apostille.docs: Hong Kong has issued apostilles since the Convention was extended to it under the UK in 1965 and continues to after 1997 through China; the HCCH table’s extension column for China is blank, so the extension was not read on the table (U). Notarised provenance affidavits and powers of attorney for consignment are the usual art documents.
apostille.authority: High Court Registry, Hong Kong Judiciary (U).
apostille.time: Same day to two working days (U).

cites.rule: Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance (Cap. 586), AFCD. From 31 Dec 2021 import, re-export and commercial possession of elephant ivory are banned and all ivory possession licences have lapsed; only antique ivory (removed from the wild before 1 Jul 1925, significantly altered, not a hunting trophy) may be traded, with a qualified appraisal or accredited lab dating as proof. Maximum penalty HK$10m and 10 years.
src: HK Government press release, ivory trade ban takes effect, 31 Dec 2021

aml.rule: AMLO (Cap. 615) was extended on 1 Apr 2023 to dealers in precious metals and stones: Hong Kong dealers register with Customs before carrying out transactions of HK$120,000 or more; non-Hong Kong dealers (e.g. at fairs) instead report any cash transaction of HK$120,000 or more within a day. Art dealers and auction houses are not covered; the AMLO extension did not reach art.
aml.asks: The houses apply their group KYC (ID, address, beneficial owner, source of funds) as policy, not statute (U).
src: HK Customs, Dealers in Precious Metals and Stones regime effective 1 Apr 2023

sanctions.rule: Hong Kong gives effect only to UN Security Council sanctions through the United Nations Sanctions Ordinance; it has adopted no Russia sanctions, though HK banks screen for US and EU exposure in practice (U).

freeport.rule: No freeport is needed: zero duty and no VAT leave bonded storage without a tax function. Collectors use private secure storage for security and climate control only (U).

export.law: No export permit for works of art; Singapore has no export-control statute for privately owned art (the National Heritage Board Act covers national monuments and public collections) — U.
export.needs: A Customs OUT permit via TradeNet is lodged by the forwarder; no cultural licence. CITES permit from NParks for listed species (U).
export.authority: Singapore Customs (TradeNet); NParks (CITES).
export.fee: Permit fee c.S$2.88 per TradeNet declaration (U).
export.temporary: ATA carnets: goods may stay up to 6 months within the carnet’s validity; no permit needed unless controlled; GST is charged on the selling price if a carnet item is sold; carnets for Singapore exporters are issued by the Singapore International Chamber of Commerce.
export.note: Carnet rules read on Singapore Customs (V); the no-export-permit position is U.

import.duty: No customs duty on works of art (only liquor, tobacco, petroleum and motor vehicles are dutiable) — U.
import.overlays: None.
import.vat: GST charged on the CIF value plus duty at import; rate 9% since 1 Jan 2024 (rate from memory, U). Carnet imports are GST-free unless sold.

apostille.docs: Party since 16 Sep 2021 (accession 18 Jan 2021). Notarised provenance affidavits, powers of attorney and company documents are apostilled for use abroad; incoming apostilled documents are accepted without embassy legalisation.
apostille.authority: Singapore Academy of Law (U).
apostille.time: Same day to a few working days (U).
apostille.note: Status read on HCCH (V); authority, fee and time are U.

cites.rule: NParks is the CITES authority under the Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act; domestic trade in elephant ivory banned from 1 Sep 2021 — from memory (U).

aml.rule: Precious Stones and Precious Metals (Prevention of Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing) Act 2019 regulates PSMD dealers (registration; cash transactions of S$20,000 or more reported). Art dealers and auction houses are not obliged entities — from memory (U).
aml.asks: House KYC as policy (U).

sanctions.rule: Singapore imposed its own measures on Russia in March 2022 (export controls on military and dual-use goods, electronics; restrictions on dealings with designated banks); art is not within them — from memory (U).

freeport.rule: Le Freeport (Changi; opened May 2010 as Singapore Freeport; c.22,500 m² over three storeys; a planned 24,000 m² phase 2 never built) was sold in 2022 to Wu Jihan for US$28m, well below its c.US$100m build cost, and continues as duty- and GST-suspended secure storage for art, precious metals and collectibles (The Reserve, 14 Oct 2024).
src: The Reserve, Le Freeport overview, 14 Oct 2024
freeport.note: The brief expected a 2024 sale; the source dates the sale to 2022.

export.law: Law on the Protection of Cultural Relics (revised Nov 2024, in force 1 Mar 2025 — U). Relics leave only after examination by a provincial cultural-relics export examination agency, which seals and permits each item. Cut-offs from memory (U): pre-1911 relics generally barred; 1911–1949 works restricted. NCHA’s notice of 5 May 2023 lists artists who died after 1911 in 8 categories (calligraphy and painting, ceramics, sculpture, fans, embroidery, seals, lacquer and more) whose works, or representative works, may not be exported.
export.needs: Examination certificate and export seal for anything that may be a cultural relic; contemporary works by living artists leave on an ordinary customs declaration.
export.authority: National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) and provincial examination agencies; China Customs.
export.temporary: ATA carnets accepted (CCPIT/China Chamber of International Commerce issues) — U. Loans abroad of museum relics need NCHA/State Council approval (U).
src: China Justice Observer, NCHA restricted export list of works by artists who died after 1911, May 2023
export.note: The 2023 list is sourced; the general 1911/1949 cut-offs and the 2024 law revision are from memory.

import.duty: MFN duty on works of art reported at up to 6% depending on medium; a cut to 1% could not be confirmed this session. Retaliatory tariffs on US-origin art since 2019: 20% on paintings, sculpture, photography and installation, 16% on collages, 11% on prints (West Bund 2023 guide via The Art Newspaper).
import.overlays: The US-origin surcharge above; auction imports also bear the comprehensive tax (U).
import.vat: 13% import VAT (down from 16% in 2019) on duty-paid value.
src: The Art Newspaper, tariffs on art and China–US relations, 26 Dec 2023
import.note: Rates as of Dec 2023; no 2026 official tariff schedule opened.

apostille.docs: Party since 7 Nov 2023 (accession 8 Mar 2023; some states objected, shown as A** on the HCCH table). Notarised provenance affidavits, powers of attorney and company papers are apostilled; foreign apostilled documents no longer need Chinese consular legalisation, except for objecting states.
apostille.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and authorised provincial Foreign Affairs Offices (U).

cites.rule: Endangered Species Import and Export Management Office (National Forestry and Grassland Administration) issues permits; domestic commercial ivory processing and trade banned from 31 Dec 2017 — from memory (U).

aml.rule: Anti-Money Laundering Law revised 8 Nov 2024, in force 1 Jan 2025, extends obligations to ‘specific non-financial institutions’ to be designated (real estate, precious metals, accountants and lawyers); art dealers and auction houses not designated as of 2026 — from memory (U).
aml.asks: Auction houses verify ID and collect a bidder deposit; source-of-funds checks are not statutory (U).

sanctions.rule: China has no Russia sanctions; large Chinese banks nonetheless screen for US secondary-sanctions exposure and have refused some Russia-linked payments (U).

freeport.rule: Bonded art storage operates in the Shanghai free-trade zone (the West Bund art bonded warehouse, whose 2023 import/export guide The Art Newspaper cites) and in Beijing’s Tianzhu comprehensive bonded zone; works may be shown at fairs under bond and pay duty and VAT only on release to the mainland. Fees not published (U).
src: The Art Newspaper, 26 Dec 2023 (West Bund guide)

export.law: Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties: National Treasures, Important Cultural Properties and other authorised important fine arts may not be exported as a rule. Antique fine arts leaving Japan need the Agency for Cultural Affairs’ certificate (Kobijutsuhin yushutsu kansa shomei) confirming the item is not designated, which speeds customs clearance. Other art exports freely.
export.needs: ACA export examination certificate for antique fine arts; nothing for contemporary art.
export.authority: Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunkacho).
export.temporary: ATA carnets accepted (Japan Commercial Arbitration Association issues) — U.
src: Agency for Cultural Affairs, international exchange of cultural properties

import.duty: 0% on chapter 97 (U).
import.overlays: None.
import.vat: 10% consumption tax on import value plus duty (U).

apostille.docs: Party since 27 Jul 1970 (ratified 28 May 1970). Ministry of Foreign Affairs apostilles notarised and official documents (U).
apostille.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Tokyo and Osaka (U).

cites.rule: METI issues CITES import/export approvals; domestic ivory trade continues under registration (U).

aml.rule: Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds covers dealers in precious metals and stones, not art dealers; antique dealers are licensed under the Secondhand Articles Dealer Act (U).
aml.asks: House KYC as policy (U).

sanctions.rule: Japan bans export of luxury goods to Russia, works of art included (U).

freeport.rule: No art freeport; bonded warehouses exist at ports and airports (U).

export.law: National heritage framework (amended 2024): ‘general movable cultural heritage’ may not leave Korea or be sold abroad without permission and appraisal by the Korea Heritage Service. Since 23 Jul 2024 only works made before 1946 fall in the category (formerly anything over 50 years old), so post-1946 Korean art exports freely.
export.needs: KHS appraisal/permit for pre-1946 items of artistic or academic value; nothing for later works.
export.authority: Korea Heritage Service (formerly Cultural Heritage Administration).
export.temporary: ATA carnets accepted (Korea Chamber of Commerce issues) — U.

import.duty: 0% on chapter 97 (U).
import.overlays: None.

apostille.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Justice (U).

moscow_case.scenario: A Russian resident with US$3m in a Russian bank wishes to buy a painting in London or New York and keep it in Washington, DC.

gates.gate: Moving the money out of Russia
gates.rule: CBR counter-sanction rules let a resident transfer up to US$1m (or equivalent) a month to a foreign bank account and US$10,000 a month through money-transfer systems (extended 1 Oct 2025–31 Mar 2026; later six-month renewals not opened). US$3m therefore takes three monthly tranches. The sending bank must still be able to reach a Western correspondent: the largest Russian banks are off SWIFT and blocked by OFAC, the EU and the UK, so the route runs through a non-sanctioned bank (U). Cash export above US$10,000 is banned (Decree 81, 1 Mar 2022; U).

EU: Reg. 833/2014 Art. 5b bars EU banks from accepting deposits above €100,000 from Russian nationals or residents (balances aggregated per bank; interest counts), unless the person holds an EU/EEA/Swiss residence permit (Art. 5b(2)). UK: no statutory deposit cap, but a Russian resident is a person ‘connected with Russia’ and banks de-risk. US: no nationality-based deposit ban; banks screen the SDN list and the 50% rule and most refuse inbound payments from Russian banks (U). A seller’s bank in London or New York must be willing to accept the funds.
src: Bank of Slovenia, FAQ on financial restrictive measures (Art. 5b)
Women Art Dealers, UK luxury goods ban (connected with Russia test)

gates.gate: The house’s KYC and sanctions screening
gates.rule: Christie’s, Sotheby’s, Phillips and Bonhams were found in 2020 to treat the agent as principal and not ask for whom he bought (Rotenberg purchases of over US$18m via Highland Ventures, Steamort and Advantage Alliance; adviser Gregory Baltser). Houses now require ID, beneficial owner, source of funds and wealth, and screen buyer and payer against OFAC, UK and EU lists including entities 50% owned by listed persons (practice, U). A Russia-resident bidder paying from a Russian bank is enhanced-due-diligence at best; the big houses have declined such bidders since 2022 (U).

gates.gate: Luxury-goods bans: sale to a Russian resident versus shipment to Russia
gates.rule: UK: since 14 Apr 2022 (reg. 46B, Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019) it is prohibited to export works of art worth £250 or more to Russia or to make them available to a person ‘connected with Russia’, a test of residence or location, not nationality; a London house therefore may not sell to a Moscow resident even for delivery to Washington. US: EAR 15 CFR 746 Supp. 5 bars export or re-export of art worth US$300 or more per unit to Russia or Belarus and to listed oligarchs; a sale to an unlisted Russian resident for delivery inside the US is not an export to Russia, so the EAR alone does not block it (U), though OFAC facilitation rules and bank refusals bite.
src: Women Art Dealers, UK luxury goods ban
gates.note: London route closed by the UK ‘connected with Russia’ test; New York route legally possible under the EAR for an unlisted buyer but commercially closed by KYC and banking.

gates.gate: Import into the United States and tax in Washington
gates.rule: Chapter 97 is duty-free; IEEPA tariffs are void (20 Feb 2026) and the 24 Jul 2026 s.301 action excludes chapter 97 (HTSUS 9903.05.86), so a UK- or US-origin painting pays no federal duty; Chinese-origin art would carry 7.5%. No CPIA restriction touches a modern painting. The District of Columbia charges a 6% use tax on tangible property brought into the District for use (rate from memory, U). An FWS declaration is needed only if the frame or materials contain CITES species.
src: Cultural Property News, chapter 97 excluded from the 2026 s.301 action, 4 Aug 2026

gates.rule: FinCEN’s alert of 16 Mar 2022 names artworks among the high-value assets (with real estate, precious metals, yachts, aircraft) used to evade Russia sanctions, and flags shell companies, parties associated with sanctioned Russians, and changes to art-insurance policies. The PSI report adds undisclosed principals behind an adviser. A Russia-resident buyer funding from Russia in tranches, buying through a company or adviser, or asking the house to ship to a third party would trip every one.

moscow_case.lawful_alternative: A Russian national who is lawfully resident outside Russia (e.g. in the UAE, Switzerland or an EU state with a residence permit, which lifts the Art. 5b deposit cap), is on no sanctions list and not 50% owned by a listed person, pays from an account outside Russia whose funds were there before 2022 or are documented post-2022 income, and buys in his own name with full source-of-wealth papers. The UK ‘connected with Russia’ test and the US EAR turn on residence and destination, not passport, so he may buy in London or New York and ship to Washington; the house still runs enhanced due diligence, and DC use tax falls due.
red_flags: Use of shell companies or an adviser who will not name the principal (PSI 2020: Highland Ventures, Steamort, Advantage Alliance; Gregory Baltser treated as principal by all four houses).
Involvement of persons, companies, law firms or institutions associated with sanctioned Russian individuals or companies (FinCEN alert, 16 Mar 2022).
Purchase of high-value assets, including artworks, real estate, precious metals and jewellery, yachts and aircraft, by or for sanctioned Russian parties or their proxies (FinCEN alert).
Purchase or termination of insurance policies on artwork, real estate or valuables linked to sanctioned Russian parties or their proxies (FinCEN alert).

Payment in monthly tranches that track the CBR’s US$1m limit, payment from a party other than the buyer, or routing through a third-country bank newly opened for the purpose (inference from the CBR limits; house practice, U).

insurance.f: Atlas Magazine (17 Oct 2025): paintings in permanent collections cost 0.1%–0.5% of agreed value a year to insure; ‘nail-to-nail’ cover for temporary exhibitions runs at 0.8–1‰ (0.08–0.1%) of value and can be added as an extension to a permanent-collection policy.
insurance.unit: % of agreed value per year, permanent collections

insurance.f: Specialist carriers named: Chubb, AXA XL, AIG Private Client Group, Hiscox and Huntington T. Block. Policies follow the work worldwide including transit, storage, framing and loans; Chubb pays up to 150% of the scheduled amount if market value has risen above it.
src: Masterworks Academy, how to insure fine art
insurance.note: No credible fine-art insurance market-size figure found; only market-research vendor pages surfaced.

insurance.f: Agreed-value policies fix a sum per scheduled work from an appraisal and pay it in full on total loss; market-value policies pay the value at time of loss. Standard exclusions: war and nuclear events, moths and vermin, gradual deterioration, routine conservation, intentional damage; flood and earthquake vary by carrier.
src: Masterworks Academy, how to insure fine art

insurance.f: Louvre theft (Sunday 19 Oct 2025): the French crown jewels taken from the Denon wing were valued at €88m (about US$102m) by the Paris prosecutor and were not privately insured. The Ministry of Culture said the state ‘is its own insurer’ for national-museum works in situ; French law bars national museums from insuring collections except on loan or in transit.
src: CBS News, stolen Louvre jewels not insured
insurance.note: A security audit cited by Radio France found 35% of Denon-wing rooms without camera coverage. No major fire or flood claim of 2025–26 was found within budget.

insurance.f: FinCEN’s March 2022 alert lists buying, maintaining or cancelling insurance on high-value art linked to sanctioned Russian elites — to protect its value or obtain cash for loss, theft or destruction — as a sanctions-evasion red flag.
src: Ballard Spahr on the FinCEN alert

regulation.t: US Senate PSI staff report: The Art Industry and U.S. Policies that Undermine Sanctions
regulation.b: Shell companies linked to the sanctioned Rotenberg brothers bought over US$18m of art through US auction houses and dealers from March to November 2014, via Moscow adviser Gregory Baltser. The report calls art ‘the largest legal, unregulated market in the United States’ (US$64.1bn worldwide in 2019, 44% in the US) and urges amending the Bank Secrecy Act to cover high-value art businesses, plus OFAC guidance on undisclosed principals.

regulation.t: US Treasury study on money laundering and terror finance through the trade in works of art
regulation.b: Mandated by §6110(c) of the AML Act of 2020 and published on 4 February 2022, the study found no immediate need for comprehensive AML/CFT rules on the art market and told regulators to prioritise higher-risk sectors. It named auction houses and galleries, shell companies, free-trade zones and art storage as vulnerabilities, cited US$21.3bn of US art sales in 2020, and listed four options from private-sector information sharing to expanding FinCEN rules.
src: HHR Art Law on the Treasury study
regulation.note: The Treasury PDF (home.treasury.gov/system/files/136/Treasury_Study_WoA.pdf) was not on the fetch allowlist; summary read on a law-firm page.

regulation.t: FinCEN alert on sanctions evasion by Russian elites through high-value assets
regulation.b: Issued 16 March 2022, FinCEN’s second Russia alert covers real estate, art, and precious metals and jewellery used by sanctioned elites and their proxies. Art red flags: shell companies and trusts, intermediaries such as dealers, brokers, advisers or interior designers, large cash payments in unusual currencies, buyers indifferent to recouping their outlay, and insurance manipulation on high-value art.
src: Ballard Spahr on the FinCEN alert
regulation.note: The alert number FIN-2022-Alert003 could not be confirmed: the fincen.gov PDF was not on the fetch allowlist.

regulation.t: FATF: Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market
regulation.b: Published February 2023 with input from 25 jurisdictions, the report finds that high, subjective values, a tradition of privacy, cash, intermediaries, shell companies and free-zone storage make the market attractive for laundering; it documents ISIL antiquities financing and a sanctions-evasion case using an art adviser. It recommends risk indicators (Annex A), specialised units, object databases and public–private sharing, and cites global sales of US$65.1bn in 2021.
regulation.note: fatf-gafi.org refused the fetch; the PDF was read on a Norwegian government mirror.

regulation.t: UK: OFSI guidance and mandatory sanctions reporting for art market participants
regulation.b: OFSI’s guidance (first published 14 November 2024, updated 12 May 2026) defines an art market participant as a firm registered with HMRC that trades, intermediates or stores works of art worth £10,000 or more. From 14 May 2025 AMPs and high value dealers are ‘relevant firms’ that must report designated persons and frozen assets to OFSI. Penalties run to £1m or 50% of the breach, with criminal sentences up to seven years.
src: OFSI guidance for high value dealers and art market participants

regulation.b: Published in the Official Journal on 19 June 2024 alongside the sixth AML Directive and the AMLA authority, the single rulebook applies from 10 July 2027. It brings traders in high-value goods — jewellers, watchmakers, dealers in luxury cars, planes and yachts, and cultural goods such as artworks — into the list of obliged entities and caps cash payments at €10,000 across the EU.
src: eucrim, the EU’s new AML single rulebook regulation
regulation.note: Whether free-zone and customs-warehouse operators are obliged entities was not confirmed on the regulation text.

regulation.t: US: Art Market Integrity Act (119th Congress)
regulation.b: Introduced on 29 July 2025 by Whitehouse, Fetterman, Grassley, Cassidy, Kim and McCormick, the bill would add persons trading in works of art (dealers, galleries, advisers, auction houses, custodians) to the Bank Secrecy Act’s ‘financial institution’ definition, requiring AML programmes, CTRs and SARs. It exempts artists, persons with no single transaction above US$10,000 and businesses under US$50,000 a year. No committee action by late August 2025.
src: DLA Piper, Art Market Integrity Act introduced
regulation.note: Bill number S. 2400 seen only in a search-result title; status after August 2025 and any House companion not established.

regulation.t: Panama Papers and the art market (ICIJ, 7 April 2016)
regulation.b: The Mossack Fonseca files showed Modigliani’s Seated Man with a Cane, bought at Christie’s London in 1996 for US$3.2m, held by Panamanian International Art Center, solely owned by David Nahmad since 2014 despite the family’s denials in court. They also showed Niue company Simsbury, under power of attorney of Christie’s top shareholder Joe Lewis, buying the core Ganz paintings for US$168m before their US$206.5m sale in 1997, and tied the Goulandris collection to Panamanian Wilton Trading.

stories.h: Sotheby’s sells US$700m of bonds backed by art loans
stories.s: Sotheby’s Financial Services priced a four-class, US$700m asset-backed securitisation of art-secured loans on 17 April 2024, upsized on institutional demand, with Morningstar DBRS expected to rate the senior notes AAA (sf). The house said it had originated over US$10bn of loans since inception and could lend up to US$250m against a single collection.
stories.o: Sotheby’s press release via AAP/PR Newswire

stories.h: Abu Dhabi’s ADQ puts US$1bn into Sotheby’s
stories.s: On 30 October 2024 Sotheby’s announced a US$1bn investment from Abu Dhabi sovereign fund ADQ, which became a minority shareholder alongside Patrick Drahi. The house framed it as support for expansion in the Middle East after over US$3bn of sales in the first half of 2024.
stories.note: Stake size and use of proceeds for debt not given on the page.

stories.h: Christie’s projects US$6.2bn for 2025; Sotheby’s US$7bn
stories.s: Christie’s projected 2025 global sales of US$6.2bn, up 6%, with auctions at US$4.7bn (+8%, including US$234m from Gooding) and private sales flat at US$1.5bn; luxury rose 17% to US$795m. Sotheby’s projected US$7bn, up 17%, with fine art up 15% to US$4.3bn and luxury up 22% to US$2.7bn; both houses are private and do not disclose profits.
stories.note: Article day not shown; projections announced after the November 2025 Klimt sale. Buyer’s-premium changes and margins not covered.

stories.h: Bank of America’s art loan book hits a record as the rich borrow instead of selling
stories.s: With the May 2024 New York auctions down about 23% by value, Bank of America said new art-backed credit lines were up more than 14% year on year and its art loan book was at a record, lending at 50% LTV against collections of US$10m or more at SOFR plus a spread. Deloitte put outstanding art loans at over US$36bn for 2024.

stories.h: Louvre crown jewels, valued at €88m, were not insured
stories.s: After the 19 October 2025 heist, France’s Ministry of Culture confirmed the stolen jewels carried no private insurance because the state insures its own national collections in situ. The Paris prosecutor valued the loss at €88m (about US$102m), and an audit found 35% of Denon-wing rooms without camera coverage.

stories.h: Senators move to put art dealers under the Bank Secrecy Act
stories.s: A bipartisan group led by Sheldon Whitehouse and Chuck Grassley introduced the Art Market Integrity Act on 29 July 2025 to impose AML programmes and suspicious-activity reporting on art dealers, advisers and auction houses, exempting artists and businesses under US$50,000 a year. It would align the US with the UK, EU and Switzerland; no committee action had been reported by late August 2025.

stories.h: UK art market participants must now report sanctions breaches to OFSI
stories.s: From 14 May 2025 UK art market participants and high value dealers became ‘relevant firms’ obliged to tell OFSI when they know or suspect a client is a designated person or holds frozen assets. OFSI’s guidance, updated 12 May 2026, warns of storage facilities, intermediaries and offshore payments, and penalties of up to £1m or 50% of a breach.

stories.h: Bouvier and Rybolovlev settle their nine-year freeport feud
stories.s: Geneva prosecutor Yves Bertossa closed the criminal case on 7 December 2023 after both sides agreed on 20 November to withdraw all complaints under a confidential settlement; Rybolovlev had alleged Bouvier overcharged him by €1.1bn on 38 works bought for about €2bn in 2003–14. The Monaco strand ran into 2025, with the Court of Appeal’s advisory chamber due to rule on 27 February 2025 after a 2024 ECHR finding.
stories.note: Monaco outcome after Feb 2025 not established; Sotheby’s New York verdict (Jan 2024) not on the opened pages. Second source: https://www.monaco-tribune.com/en/2024/12/rybolovlev-bouvier-affair-the-final-act/

stories.h: Inigo Philbrick out of prison after under four years of a seven-year term
stories.s: The dealer who pleaded guilty to wire fraud in November 2021 for an US$86m scheme of selling overlapping shares in the same works was sentenced to seven years in May 2022 and released in early 2024 (February per the Daily Mail, January per Vanity Fair) to home confinement and two years’ supervised release.
stories.note: Exact release date differs between the two outlets cited by the article.

stories.h: Court gives David Nahmad 30 days to hand over the Panama Papers Modigliani
stories.s: On 16 June 2026 Justice Joel M. Cohen of the New York Supreme Court gave Nahmad 30 days to return Modigliani’s Seated Man with a Cane (1918), valued at about US$30m, to Philippe Maestracci, grandson of dealer Oscar Stettiner, after ruling on 6 April 2026 that it must be restituted. Nahmad, who bought it for US$3.2m in 1996 through a Panamanian company exposed in the Panama Papers, will appeal.
stories.note: Panama company link from ICIJ 2016; outcome of the appeal after June 2026 not established.

stories.h: Vancouver developer accused of pledging art to a US bank while his firm collapsed
stories.s: Investors suing Coromandel Properties CEO Jerry Zhong in British Columbia allege he bought C$6.9m (US$4.9m) of art — by Basquiat, Calleja, Condo, Gilliam and others — while the firm was in distress, then used it to secure a US bank credit line of up to C$3.3m that he drew for his own use. Coromandel’s collapse left C$700m of debt; Zhong denies the claims and the art’s whereabouts are unknown.
stories.note: No 2026 lender failure found; this is the only 2026 art-collateral case opened.

stories.h: Masterworks: 29 exits from 500-plus paintings, and a 17% ‘median’ under scrutiny
stories.s: By June 2026 the fractional platform had deployed about US$1.2bn into over 500 paintings and sold 29, with net annualised returns on exits from 4.1% to 77.3% and a flagship Basquiat returning 6.3% a year over 3.8 years. Fees are 1.5% a year plus 20% of profits and a purchase markup of about 10–11%; Masterworks itself warns its internal secondary market ‘frequently lacks liquidity’.

sculpture.f: Artprice’s 2025 report could not be opened in full, so sculpture’s share of auction turnover and lots is unconfirmed; the press release gives only totals (US$11.1bn turnover, 867,000 lots, 32% unsold).

Giacometti’s Grande tête mince (1954/55), consigned by the Soloviev Foundation with an estimate above US$70m and no guarantee, failed to sell at Sotheby’s New York on 13 May 2025 when bidding stalled near US$64m; the sale made US$186.4m with fees against a US$170m–248m estimate, 83% sold.

Brancusi’s Danaïde sold for US$107.6m at Christie’s New York on 18 May 2026 from the estate of S.I. Newhouse, the second-highest auction price for a sculpture after Giacometti’s L’Homme au doigt (US$141.3m, Christie’s, 11 May 2015); Koons’s Rabbit (US$91.1m) and Bourgeois’s Spider (US$32.1m) both date from 15 May 2019.

sculpture.f: Christie’s New York sold 70 animal bronzes and stone works from Dorothée Lalanne’s collection for US$58.9m in October 2024 against a US$16m–23m estimate; Très Grand Centaure made US$7.5m and Très Grand Ours US$6.1m, 97% of lots beat their high estimates, and buyers were over 50% from the Americas, 30% Europe, 15% Asia.

Christie’s design-sale record is the Marie Lalanne collection of 7 December 2022 in New York: US$77.0m, 100% sold, 18 lots above US$1m, led by Âne Planté at US$8.4m; prices averaged 319% of low estimates.

sculpture.f: François-Xavier Lalanne’s Hippopotame Bar sold for US$31.4m at Sotheby’s New York in December 2025 (estimate US$7m–10m), a record for the artist and the highest price for any design work at auction; Lalanne lots in that sale made about US$38m, and the Pauline Karpidas sale at Sotheby’s London in September 2025 brought nearly US$18.5m of Lalanne.

ArtTactic puts collectible-design auction sales at US$172m in the first half of 2025, up 20.4% from US$143m in H1 2024; Sotheby’s December 2025 design week at the Met Breuer totalled US$58.4m, with the Schlumberger collection at US$50.2m (94% sold, bidders from 40 countries).
