theses.t: Rarity pays, but only for the proven
theses.thesis: The money will keep concentrating on the few dozen Russian avant-garde works with unbroken Western provenance, as Popova’s October 2026 record showed. With Russian buyers and consignors shut out since 2022 and the fakes problem unresolved, the school trades as scarce Western modernism, not as a national market.

evidence.f: Popova’s Painterly Architectonic (1918) made £6.2m hammer (£7.6m with fees) at Christie’s London on 14 October 2026, over three times its £1.8m low estimate and nearly four times her 2007 record.
Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben (1907), restituted in June 2023 to the Lewenstein heirs, sold for £27m hammer (£31.6m with fees) in the same sale, above its £25m high estimate and third-party guaranteed.
Kandinsky’s record is Murnau mit Kirche II (1910), £37.2m ($44.55m) at Sotheby’s London on 1 March 2023, a restituted work; the previous record was £33m ($39.7m) in 2017.

Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Bonhams cancelled their June 2022 London Russian sales; Russian art sales at the two majors’ London rooms were £37.7m ($49.6m) in 2021, under 1% of turnover (Art Market Research).
src: Reuters via The Business Standard, 17 Mar 2022

evidence.f: The authenticity problem is on the record: Russian critics challenged Ghent’s museum over dubious avant-garde works (28 Feb 2018), Museum Ludwig tested 22 falsely attributed works (2020) and French authorities seized avant-garde paintings believed stolen (2 Apr 2024).
src: The Art Newspaper keyword page: Russian avant-garde

evidence.f: An adviser in the room called the Popova result ‘probably not a surprise because her work is so rare’; the article names no buyer and describes no wider Russian avant-garde demand.

risks: Fakes: the 2018 Ghent (Toporovski) affair and the 2020 Museum Ludwig review keep buyers to works with pre-1990 Western exhibition history, which shrinks the tradable pool further.
Sanctions: the Russian buyer and consignor base is absent and may stay so; a thaw would add supply before it added demand.
Supply is in museums: the great works sit in the Tretyakov, the Russian Museum, the Stedelijk and MoMA; what trades is mostly works on paper and the odd restituted canvas.
Restitution-driven supply (both 2023 and 2026 Kandinsky records) is lumpy and cannot be planned for.

record.note: Day inferred from ‘Wednesday’ in an article dated 3 March 2023. Goncharova’s record was not opened in this session.

theses.t: Nonconformists wait for a saleroom to return
theses.thesis: Soviet nonconformist and 20th-century Russian art lost its Western saleroom when London’s Russian Week stopped in 2022; prices now form in a thin private and online trade. Over twenty years the case is museum-led rediscovery of Kabakov, Bulatov, Rabin and Weisberg, but until a major house relists the category the terminal reads it as cool with a long option attached.

evidence.f: Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Bonhams cancelled their June 2022 Russian art sales in London; Christie’s cited the war and the legal and logistical demands of sanctions, calling its Russian market ‘relatively small’.
src: Reuters via The Business Standard, 17 Mar 2022

evidence.f: In the last full Russian Week, MacDougall’s sold £4.4m on 10 June 2021, with Bulatov’s The Vault of Heaven (2007) at £645,000 the most expensive contemporary work across four London houses that week; Christie’s took £3.1m in Russian paintings.
Most MacDougall’s lots in June 2021 went to first-time buyers bidding over the internet, which is where the category now lives.
An American adviser’s 2022 verdict, ‘you don’t want to be caught buying something coming from a Russian at this point’, still describes the compliance reflex at the major houses.
src: Reuters via The Business Standard, 17 Mar 2022

risks: Compliance: any consignor or buyer with Russian links triggers sanctions screening, so the houses avoid the category rather than price it.
No price discovery: without London’s twice-yearly sales there is no public benchmark, and private prices can be stale or inflated.
Provenance: Soviet-era export and the 1990s diaspora trade leave gaps that a museum acquisitions committee will query.
The thesis depends on Western museums re-reading the period; the current state of their buying was not established in this session.

record.note: A sale-week high, not the category record; Kabakov’s record (Beetle, Phillips London, 2008) is carried from memory and was not opened (U). MacDougall’s current sale calendar was not established.

theses.t: India: a domestic market with national-treasure walls
theses.thesis: Indian modern art will keep rising on domestic wealth, with records set in Mumbai and New Delhi rather than New York. Because the ‘national treasure’ artists cannot leave India, the top of the market is a closed pool of Indian buyers; the Progressives, who can travel, are the international play.

evidence.f: Raja Ravi Varma’s Yashoda and Krishna (1890s) made $15m hammer, $17.9m with fees (₹167.2 crore) at Saffronart Mumbai on 1 April 2026, against an $8.6–12.9m estimate, bought by Cyrus Poonawalla; a record for an Indian painting.

M.F. Husain’s Gram Yatra made $13.7m with fees at Christie’s New York in March 2025; Christie’s New York South Asian sale of 25 March 2026 made $27m, the highest for such a sale outside India, and Sotheby’s New York (24 March 2026) made $22.1m with best prices for 12 artists.

Saffronart’s 25th-anniversary sale in New Delhi on 27 September 2025 made Rs 355.77 crore from 85 lots, all sold: Gaitonde’s Untitled (1970) Rs 67.08 crore (artist record), Tyeb Mehta’s Trussed Bull (1956) Rs 56.4 crore, Husain’s Mahabharata Rs 21.6 crore, Souza Rs 20.4 crore, Raza Rs 18 crore.

Ravi Varma is one of the artists designated ‘national treasure’ under India’s 1972 antiquities and art treasures law, so his works cannot leave the country; the buyer could not have been from overseas. Christie’s plans its first live South Asian Modern sale in London in seven years.
evidence.note: The article says 11 designated artists; the commonly cited list is nine. Not resolved here.

evidence.f: The September 2025 total beat Saffronart’s April 2025 record by more than 60%, and the house called it ‘a new benchmark for the Indian art market’.

risks: The top of the market is a handful of Indian industrialists; a change in their appetite moves prices more than any global trend.
Export rules: national-treasure artists and anything over 100 years old cannot leave India, so foreign buyers are confined to the Progressives and later work.
Rupee weakness turns rupee records into flat dollar results.
Husain and Souza were prolific; attribution and condition questions grow with prices.
Annual national auction totals and the state of the new museums (KNMA’s Adjaye building, NMACC) were not confirmed in this session.

theses.t: Korea: a bottom forming beneath Dansaekhwa
theses.thesis: Korean auctions rose in 2025 for the first time in four years but remain well under half their 2021 peak, so Dansaekhwa and the post-war masters are bought at a discount to 2021–22 rather than at a top. Over ten to thirty years Frieze Seoul’s institutional traffic and museum placements argue for a steady re-rating led by Kim Whanki, Yoo Youngkuk, Park Seo-Bo and Lee Ufan.

evidence.f: Eight Korean auction houses sold 131.5bn won through November 2025, up 16.6%, the first rise in four years; domestic hammer totals had peaked at 324.2bn won in 2021, and the whole Korean art market fell from 806.6bn won (2022) to 615.1bn won (2024).

Lots fell 20% to 8,782 while eight works passed 1bn won (five in 2024); Chagall’s Bouquet de Fleurs at 9.4bn won was the highest price ever at a Korean domestic auction, and Lee Ufan’s Cow and Child made 3.52bn won (2025).

Frieze Seoul 2026 (closed 5 September) had 130+ galleries, 70,000 visitors and 178 museums; Kukje sold a 1971 Yoo Youngkuk for KRW 2.2–2.5bn ($1.6–1.8m), the highest price for a Korean artist at the fair since 2022; White Cube sold two Park Seo-Bo works at $300,000 and $190,000.

Kim Whanki’s 19-VI-71 #206 (1971) made $8.4m at Christie’s New York in November 2025 (estimate $7.5–10m); he holds the top five Korean prices, led by 05-IV-71 #200 (Universe) at HK$88m (US$11.3m) at Christie’s Hong Kong in 2019.
src: Asia News Network / The Korea Herald, 20 Nov 2025

evidence.f: South Korea’s art sales rose 6% in 2025 (Arts Economics), against Japan at −1%.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Of 154 Korean galleries and fairs surveyed in December 2025, 48.4% reported lower 2025 sales and 27.1% expected a further fall in 2026; the auction rebound has not yet reached the primary market.

risks: The won and the Korean economy drive the domestic bid; galleries expect a flat 2026.
Dansaekhwa supply is large: long careers, series production and late works dilute the scarcity premium.
Kim Whanki’s top prices are set in Hong Kong and New York, not Seoul; the Korean saleroom’s own record is a Chagall.
Western demand for Dansaekhwa after the 2014–16 wave is unproven at the top end.

src: Asia News Network / The Korea Herald, 20 Nov 2025
record.note: The source gives the year only; the day is from memory (U). The price with premium is commonly cited as HK$102m ($13.2m); unresolved here.

theses.t: China: big, flat, and splitting in two
theses.thesis: China is the world’s third market at $8.5bn but grew only about 1% in 2025 while its contemporary auction value fell 18%; the money has moved to Hong Kong evening sales and to a short list of mainland names. The terminal expects the Franco-Chinese moderns (Zao, Sanyu, Chu) to hold as blue chips, the 1990s contemporaries to lag, and the new mainland painters to be the volatile growth.

evidence.f: China’s art sales were $8.5bn in 2025, up just over 1%, a 14% global share (down one point); mainland auctions rose while Hong Kong contracted.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Contemporary auction sales in China fell 18% in the year to June 2026, though it stayed the second-largest market with about 40 million-dollar results, mainly in Hong Kong and Beijing.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

evidence.f: In 2025 Chinese modern and contemporary art made HK$1.598bn at Christie’s Hong Kong, HK$745m at Sotheby’s Hong Kong and RMB 686m at China Guardian Beijing (about 70% of the market between them); 91 lots passed 10m, 69 of them in Hong Kong.
src: Artpro, 2025 China Modern and Contemporary Art Market Report, Part 1

evidence.f: Mainland highs of 2025: Zhang Peili’s X? (1980) RMB 71.3m at China Guardian on 10 November, Huang Yuxing RMB 36.8m (13 May), Zeng Fanzhi RMB 14.03m at Yongle, Liu Ye RMB 10.35m; Zao Wou-Ki’s 1.12.81 made HK$27.6m at Poly Hong Kong in the spring.
src: Artpro, 2025 China Modern and Contemporary Art Market Report, Part 1

evidence.f: Christie’s Hong Kong 20th/21st Century autumn sales of 26–27 September 2025 made $105.5m, 96% sold by lot, led by Picasso’s Buste de femme at $25.4m (an Asia record); Greater China led the bidding and new buyers were 20%, over half of them millennials.

Since 5 May 2023 China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration has kept a restricted-export list of works by artists who died after 1911, in eight categories including painting and calligraphy; for listed artists all works or their representative works may not leave China.
src: China Justice Observer on the NCHA notice of 5 May 2023

risks: Export curbs: works by listed deceased artists bought on the mainland cannot be exported, and the list can grow; Hong Kong remains the only exit.
Capital controls and the property slump cap mainland bidding; Hong Kong’s own total contracted in 2025.
The 2000s contemporaries (Political Pop, Cynical Realism) depend on a Western demand that has not returned.
Zao Wou-Ki’s record and the Hong Kong autumn 2026 totals by house were not opened in this session.

record.note: Carried from memory and the brief; no page opened in this session. The 2025 marker with a source is Zhang Peili’s RMB 71.3m at China Guardian (S).

theses.t: Classical Chinese: the oldest money, the deepest bids
theses.thesis: Classical painting, calligraphy and works of art are where Chinese wealth bid hardest through the downturn: a Yuan handscroll made HK$250m in 2025 and Sotheby’s Asian works-of-art series was its most valuable since 2013. Supply is finite and keeps moving into museums, so the terminal expects records to keep falling at the top while the middle stays thin.

evidence.f: A Yuan dynasty handscroll by Rao Jie sold for HK$250m (US$32m) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2025, 25 times its estimate after more than 200 bids, the most valuable Chinese calligraphy sold at the house.

Sotheby’s autumn 2025 Asian Art series in Hong Kong made HK$1.4bn (US$180.37m); the Asian Works of Art series alone made HK$1.17bn (US$150m), the most valuable since 2013, with the Ise ceramics collection 99.5% sold and a Southern Song Guan dish at HK$55.88m.

The Xiao Wan Liu Tang fan paintings and calligraphy made HK$182.32m (US$23.46m) across three sales, led by Yun Shouping’s Landscape after Zhao Mengfu at HK$11.6m; the season drew the highest number of new bidders in 14 years, from 20 regions.
Mainland auction sales rose in 2025 while Hong Kong contracted, within a Chinese market of $8.5bn (+1%).
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: The NCHA’s May 2023 restricted-export list covers calligraphy and painting by named artists who died after 1911; older material falls under China’s cultural-relics export regime.
src: China Justice Observer on the NCHA notice of 5 May 2023

risks: Anything deemed a cultural relic cannot leave the mainland; the buyer’s liquidity is Hong Kong or nothing.
Attribution: scrolls, seals and colophons are the most forged objects in the Chinese market, and the top prices rest on connoisseurship rather than science.
Poly and China Guardian 2025–26 totals for classical painting were not established in this session; the mainland top end is known here only through Hong Kong.
A mainland economic or political shock would hit this segment first, since its buyers are domestic.

record.note: The terminal’s own record entry; not opened in this session. The sourced 2025 marker is the Rao Jie handscroll, HK$250m at Sotheby’s Hong Kong (V), day not given by the source.

theses.t: Gulf money, Arab moderns: the re-rating begins
theses.thesis: Arab and Iranian modernism is priced far below its museum presence: the top Arab lot of 2023 was $1.1m and Mahmoud Saïd’s 2010 record of $2.43m still stands. With Christie’s and Sotheby’s now selling in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening in December 2026, the terminal expects a decade of catching up, led by state and foundation buying.

evidence.f: Mahmoud Saïd’s Les Chadoufs (1934) made $2.43m against a $150,000–200,000 estimate at Christie’s Dubai in April 2010, the most expensive work by an Arab artist the house had sold there; the sale made about $15.1m, 86% sold.

The ten most expensive Arab works of 2023 ran from $352,800 (Etel Adnan) to $1.1m (Mohammed Al Saleem, a Saudi record, Sotheby’s, October 2023), with Saïd’s Fille à l’imprimé at $721,849 from the Dalloul collection in November 2023.
Sotheby’s Origins II in Riyadh (January 2026) made $19.5m; Safeya Binzagr’s Coffee Shop in Madina Road sold for $2.1m against a projected $1.05–1.35m, and about a third of lots went to local buyers.

A Saudi adviser says regional artists ‘still trade at 15 to 30 percent of Western peers’ with comparable museum representation; Qantara puts Middle Eastern collectors at 23% of global demand for contemporary works above $1m.

Christie’s first Abu Dhabi fine-art sale, Mawasim, on 1 November 2026 offered 70 Middle Eastern works spanning nine decades, with lenders including Sharjah’s Barjeel Art Foundation and Beirut’s Dalloul collection; the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens on 11 December 2026.
The counter-signal: Middle East contemporary auction sales fell 28% in the year to June 2026, largely in the Gulf (Artprice).
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

risks: Regional war: the Gulf sales run in the shadow of conflict and a single escalation empties the room.
State and foundation demand can stop as quickly as it started; private Gulf collectors remain few.
The great collections (Barjeel, Dalloul, Mathaf) lend rather than sell, so the secondary supply is thin and often minor.
Authentication bodies for Saïd, Guiragossian and the Baghdad moderns are young; fakes follow prices.

record.note: Day inferred from ‘last night’ in an article dated 28 April 2010. No higher price for an Arab modern was found in this session; Christie’s Abu Dhabi results of 1 November 2026 were not opened (see unconfirmed).

theses.t: Abu Dhabi and Riyadh become sale rooms
theses.thesis: Within thirty years the Gulf will be the third saleroom region after New York–London and Hong Kong: Christie’s held its first Abu Dhabi fine-art sale on 1 November 2026, Sotheby’s sells in Riyadh and opens in Abu Dhabi in December, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens on 11 December 2026. Museums are the demand; the open question is whether private Gulf wealth follows them.

evidence.f: Christie’s chief executive Bonnie Brennan, in Abu Dhabi for the 1 November 2026 sale, said ‘the market can sustain two centres’ and that the house would ‘love to have a more regularly scheduled calendar of sales’ there; Rothko, Kandinsky and Picasso lots were shown in Abu Dhabi before their New York sales.

Christie’s first-half 2026 auction sales were $3.5bn, up 71%, and millennials and Gen Z were 47% of its new clients; the Abu Dhabi season also brings Frieze’s first fair in November and the Guggenheim opening on 11 December 2026.

Saudi Arabia targets culture at about 3% of GDP by 2030 (roughly SR180bn, $48bn) from SR60bn in 2023; about 20 museums are planned, the Saudi Museum of Contemporary Art has opened and Colnaghi is opening in Riyadh.

Saudi private wealth exceeds $2.4trn but Saudi buyers were 0.01% of high-value art purchases, and Saudi family offices put about 1% into art against about 7% globally (Qantara); Sotheby’s Origins II in Riyadh (January 2026) made $19.5m.
Middle East contemporary auction sales fell 28% in the year to June 2026, largely in the Gulf (Artprice), so the new rooms open into a soft regional cycle.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

risks: War in the region is the dominant risk to every Gulf date on the calendar.
Demand is state-led; a budget turn in Riyadh or Abu Dhabi would remove the marginal bidder.
Four hubs (Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Riyadh, Doha) compete for the same collectors and lenders, which can dilute each of them.
Import, VAT and free-port rules for the new rooms, and the results of Christie’s 1 November sale and Art Basel Qatar, were not opened in this session.

record.note: The source gives January 2026 only, and does not call it a record; the previous Saudi record cited was Al Saleem’s $1.1m (2023).

theses.t: Latin America: Surrealism’s women lead a re-rating
theses.thesis: Kahlo’s $54.7m in November 2025 made a Latin American the most expensive woman artist at auction, and the Surrealist collections sold around her went white-glove. With Brazilian galleries up 21% in 2025 and SP-Arte growing, the terminal expects Mexican and Brazilian modernism to re-rate over two decades, though the supply of Kahlo and Tarsila is tiny and partly locked at home.

evidence.f: Kahlo’s El sueño (La cama) (1940) made $47m hammer, $54.6m with fees (reported as $54.7m) at Sotheby’s New York on 20 November 2025, above a $40m low estimate, passing O’Keeffe’s $44.4m (2014) as the record for a woman artist and for a Latin American work.

The 24-lot ‘Exquisite Corpus’ Surrealist collection made $98m with fees (estimate $66.7–98.9m), all sold, with 11 of 24 lots above high estimate and records for Dorothea Tanning ($2.7m hammer), Bellmer and Paalen; Sotheby’s Helena Newman cited ‘the surge in interest in the movement in the last several years’.

SP-Arte’s 22nd edition (8–12 April 2026, São Paulo) had over 180 galleries, studios and institutions; the Art Basel and UBS report records a 21% rise in Brazilian galleries’ 2025 sales, and the fair’s design section grew from 23 to 64 stands since 2016.
The New York Times noted that O’Keeffe’s 2014 price is about $60.5m in today’s money, so the Kahlo record is a nominal, not a real, high for a woman artist.

risks: Mexico treats Kahlo and Rivera as national patrimony, so works inside Mexico do not come to New York; the auction supply is the pre-war diaspora of pictures and little else.
Brazil’s and Mexico’s currencies and politics set the local bid; the Brazilian gallery rise is one year of data.
Carrington’s $28.5m (2024), Tarsila’s and Botero’s records were not opened in this session and are carried as unconfirmed.
The Surrealism wave since the 2024 centenary can crest; the 2025 records came from two single-owner collections.

theses.t: Africa: 0.1% of the market, after the boom
theses.thesis: African art is about 0.1% of global auction value and its 2020–22 stars fell with the under-40 segment, down 26.6% in the year to June 2026. The long case rests on museums (Tate buying Boafo at 1-54, MOWAA in Benin City) and on the moderns, Enwonwu, Stern, Sekoto, El Anatsui, whose supply is finite; the terminal reads cool now, warming over twenty years.

evidence.f: African art is roughly $72m a year at auction against a $67.8bn global market, about 0.1% (ArtTactic figures as cited); Strauss & Co’s year was R475.5m (about $26m) and its Nairobi sale about $230,000, 86% sold.
src: MoMAA, Where is Africa in the 2025 auction records?
evidence.note: Secondary aggregator; the ArtTactic and Strauss figures were not checked at source.

evidence.f: Julie Mehretu’s Walkers With the Dawn and Morning made $10.7m at Sotheby’s New York in November 2023, the highest auction price for an African-born artist; Akunyili Crosby reached $4.74m (2022), El Anatsui $2.2m, Enwonwu’s Tutu $1.67m (2018), and Irma Stern’s Malay (Black Headdress) (1946) R21.7m (about $1.26m) at Strauss & Co.
src: MoMAA, Where is Africa in the 2025 auction records?

evidence.f: Auction sales of artists under 40 fell 26.6% in the year to June 2026 while contemporary art overall rose 6%; Artprice says the correction is ‘bringing prices back toward more sustainable levels’.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

evidence.f: Tate acquired an Amoako Boafo painting at 1-54 Marrakech in early 2025; at Christie’s London on 14 October 2026 Portia Zvavahera set a record at £307,200 and Igshaan Adams sold at £96,000.
src: MoMAA, Where is Africa in the 2025 auction records?

risks: Infrastructure: few auction houses, weak currencies (rand, naira) and costly shipping keep most trade in London, New York and Paris.
The 2020–22 cohort (Boafo and peers) was bought for resale; its price fall since 2021 was not quantified in this session.
Records cluster in three Western salerooms’ themed sales, which can be cut when totals fall.
Export and heritage rules in Nigeria and South Africa for the moderns were not established here.

record.work: Walkers With the Dawn and Morning (2008)
src: MoMAA, Where is Africa in the 2025 auction records?
record.note: The source gives November 2023; the day is from memory (U).

theses.t: Japan and Vietnam: Asia’s next blue chips
theses.thesis: Hong Kong’s autumn 2026 sales put Japanese and Vietnamese pictures at the top: Nara’s Present made HK$71.7m, Japanese artists sold 100%, and Vu Cao Dam set the Vietnamese record at HK$29m. With Kusama’s death closing her supply and Foujita entering single-artist sales, the terminal expects Japan to anchor Asian demand and Vietnamese and Indonesian moderns to re-rate over two decades.

evidence.f: At Sotheby’s Hong Kong on 28 September 2026 Nara’s Present (1994) made HK$71.66m (US$9.32m) and The Crated Room in Iceland/Drawing Room (2009) HK$61.9m; Japanese artists sold 100% across both evening sales.

Vu Cao Dam’s Conversation d’élégantes au jardin (1939) made HK$28.96m (US$3.76m) after 14 bids, the highest price for a Vietnamese work at auction; Tetsuya Ishida’s Can’t Fly Anymore (1996) made HK$12.16m above its high estimate.

The Foujita Lexicon (Lewis collection) was a white-glove sale at HK$67.2m (US$8.74m), Sotheby’s first single-artist auction in Asia; Kusama’s Infinity-Nets (LHLUJ) (2017) made HK$15.36m (US$2.0m), above its high estimate.

A year earlier Nara’s Can’t Wait ’til the Night Comes (2012) made HK$79.9m at Sotheby’s Hong Kong (28 September 2025), and at Christie’s Hong Kong that week Thai, Vietnamese, Filipino, Japanese and Korean artists sold 100%.
src: Artpro, 2025 China Modern and Contemporary Art Market Report, Part 1

evidence.f: Utamaro’s Fukagawa in Snow made HK$55.27m (US$7.1m) in 2025, a record for the artist and for ukiyo-e painting, and the Okada Museum of Art sale made HK$688m (US$88m) over 125 lots.
Yayoi Kusama died in August 2026 aged 97; the effect on her prices is not yet measurable.
evidence.note: Seen only in search-result headlines of 27 August 2026 (Artprice, ArtDependence, Tribune); no page opened. The terminal records 14 August 2026. Japan’s domestic market fell 1% in 2025 (Arts Economics, V).

risks: Concentration: two artists, Nara and Kusama, carry most of the Japanese total; Kusama’s very large supply of prints and late works can swamp the scarcity effect of her death.
Vietnamese and Indonesian moderns have a long fakes history (Hanoi school, Affandi), and few catalogues raisonnés.
Japan’s own market is flat (−1% in 2025); the demand is Hong Kong and Chinese money, not Tokyo.
Gutai, Affandi, Hendra Gunawan and Le Pho records were not opened in this session.

record.note: Record for a Vietnamese work. Nara’s own record (Knife Behind Back, Sotheby’s Hong Kong, 2019) was not opened (U).

theses.t: Women artists: from discount to premium
theses.thesis: Women are now 45% of the artists dealers show and 37% of dealer sales by value, and the records of 2025–26 (Kahlo $54.7m; Popova, Riley and Hepworth in one October week) came from scarcity meeting museum re-reading. The terminal expects the gap to male peers to keep closing for thirty years, fastest for modernists with small, catalogued bodies of work.

evidence.f: In 2025 women were 45% of artists represented by dealers (up 4 points) and 37% of dealer sales by value (up 2); primary-market galleries made 44% of sales from women’s work.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Kahlo’s El sueño (La cama) made $54.7m with fees at Sotheby’s New York on 20 November 2025, the record for a woman artist, passing O’Keeffe’s $44.4m of 2014; Dorothea Tanning set a record at $2.7m hammer the same night.
On 14 October 2026 Christie’s London set records for Popova (£7.6m with fees), Bridget Riley (£5.2m with fees), Hepworth as a painter (£537,600) and Portia Zvavahera (£307,200).
Li Hei Di set a record at HK$3.33m after 18 bids at Sotheby’s Hong Kong on 28 September 2026, and Safeya Binzagr’s Coffee Shop in Madina Road made $2.1m at Sotheby’s Riyadh in January 2026.
At Frieze Seoul 2026 Lehmann Maupin placed a Kim Yun Shin painting with a Korean museum and David Zwirner placed two Mamma Andersson paintings with a South Korean museum.

risks: ‘Women artists’ is a basket, not a school; the index rises because of a few estates (Kahlo, Mitchell, Carrington) and can fall with them.
In real terms the ceiling has barely moved: O’Keeffe’s 2014 price is about $60.5m today, above the Kahlo record.
The ultra-contemporary women of 2021–22 sit inside the under-40 segment, down 26.6% in the year to June 2026.
Saville’s 2025 show and record, and the Mitchell, Krasner and Agnes Martin records, were not opened in this session.

theses.t: Sculpture: estates sell, speculation does not
theses.thesis: Three-dimensional work now splits by provenance: Lalanne’s estate sold 70 animals for $58.9m in October 2024 with 97% of lots above high estimate, Hepworth led Christie’s Modern British week in October 2026, but the unguaranteed $70m Giacometti stalled at $64m in May 2025. The terminal expects collectible design and fresh estates to keep gaining share, while trophy bronzes need a guarantor.

evidence.f: Christie’s New York sold 70 François-Xavier Lalanne sculptures from Dorothée Lalanne on 10 October 2024 for $58.9m, 97% of lots above their high estimates; Très Grand Centaure (2001) made $7.5m against a $1.2m high estimate and Très Grand Ours (2009) $6.1m.
evidence.note: The article does not state the year; it is October 2024 from the search context and the terminal.

evidence.f: Lalanne bidders came 54% from the Americas, 15% from Asia Pacific and 31% from Europe; his record remains Léopard I (2001) at $9.6m in 2021.

Giacometti’s Grande tête mince (1954/55), estimated above $70m and unguaranteed, stalled at about $64m and failed to sell at Sotheby’s New York on 13 May 2025; the Modern evening sale made $186.4m with fees against a $170–248m estimate, 83% sold, with 26 of the sold lots guaranteed.
The same night a Frank Lloyd Wright lamp made almost $7.5m with fees after an 11-minute bidding war, a record for Wright, and a smaller Giacometti sold within estimate at $6.8m with fees.
Hepworth set a painting record of £537,600 at Christie’s London on 14 October 2026; at Frieze Seoul 2026 Thaddaeus Ropac sold an Antony Gormley for $1m.

risks: Editions and posthumous casts: for Giacometti, Rodin and Lalanne the cast, the number and the foundry decide the price, and estates can add supply.
Lalanne’s run is partly fashion (the Jacquemus staging); design cycles turn faster than painting cycles.
Sculpture’s share of auction turnover (Artprice) could not be read in this session; the Hepworth sculpture record of 21 October 2026 and Giacometti’s $141.3m record were not opened.
Trophy lots without guarantees have failed in public, which deters consignors and pushes them to private sales.

record.note: Top lot of the Dorothée Lalanne sale, not the artist’s record (Léopard I, $9.6m, 2021). The sculpture record, Giacometti’s L’Homme au doigt ($141.3m, Christie’s New York, 11 May 2015), is in the terminal and was not opened here (U).

theses.t: Old Masters: scarcity, one buyer, and sleepers
theses.thesis: The Old Master market is thin but its top is firm because the great names are nearly all in museums: a re-identified Rembrandt made £6.75m in December 2025 and went to Thomas Kaplan’s Leiden Collection, his 18th, and a Rembrandt lion drawing made nearly $18m in February 2026. The terminal expects the few tradable masterworks to rise with Gulf and Asian museum building while the middle market keeps shrinking.

evidence.f: Rembrandt’s Saint John on Patmos (c.1661), long thought to show his son Titus, sold at Sotheby’s London in December 2025 for £6.75m (about $9m); the buyer, revealed on 28 September 2026, was Thomas Kaplan, and it is the 18th Rembrandt the Leiden Collection has acquired in about two decades.

Kaplan’s Rembrandt drawing Young Lion Resting (c.1638–42) made nearly $18m at Sotheby’s New York in February 2026, against a November 2025 expectation of about $15m; the proceeds endow the Panthera wildlife charity.

Kaplan attributes the strength of Rembrandt masterworks to ‘extreme scarcity’, allows that his buying may affect prices ‘in specific moments’, and sellers now expect him to bid, which can push prices up.
Across fine art, 56% of offline auction value in 2025 came from lots of $1m or more, while online-only sales fell to $9.2bn, the lowest since 2019; the top is where the Old Master money sits.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

risks: Attribution risk runs both ways: a sleeper can be upgraded (the Saint John) or a bought picture downgraded by a scholar’s committee.
One-buyer dependence: if Kaplan stops bidding, the Rembrandt market loses its floor.
Export licensing in the UK, Italy and France can stop a sale or delay it for years; the Gulf and Asian museums that would buy are abroad.
Old Master sale totals for 2025–26 were not established in this session; the Salvator Mundi record is in the terminal, not opened here.

record.note: Not a record: a 2025–26 marker. The Old Master record, Salvator Mundi at $450.3m (Christie’s New York, 15 Nov 2017), is in the terminal (U here). The day comes from the 4 December 2025 report the article links.

theses.t: Ultra-contemporary: the correction is the opportunity
theses.thesis: Artists under 40 lost 26.6% of auction value in the year to June 2026 while the rest of contemporary rose 6%, and Artprice calls the correction a return to sustainable prices. The terminal expects the 2020–22 cohort to trade below its peaks for a decade; the thirty-year winners will be the few with museum shows, so buying should follow institutions, not auction momentum.

evidence.f: Contemporary art (artists born after 1945) rose 6% in auction value and 9% in volume in the year to 30 June 2026, after three years of decline, with a record number of lots sold for the sixth year; the roughly $100m gain was all recorded in the United States.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

evidence.f: Sales of artists under 40 fell 26.6% in the same year and the gap to the rest of the market widened; the market ‘returned decisively to growth’ without higher prices.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

evidence.f: Artprice’s annual report of 10 March 2026 says market stability now ‘rests primarily on lower-priced transactions’, that galleries are fragile with closures and restructuring, and that millennial and Gen Z buyers compare prices online and favour affordable works.
src: Artprice, The Art Market Report 2025 (Spanish edition), 10 Mar 2026

evidence.f: Young names still clear at modest levels: at Sotheby’s Hong Kong on 28 September 2026 Li Hei Di set a record at HK$3.33m with 18 bids and Yu Nishimura’s at night (2022) made HK$2.3m, over double its high estimate.
Online-only sales, the channel that carried the 2021 boom, fell to $9.2bn in 2025, 15% of the market and the lowest since 2019.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

risks: A new speculative cohort (Asian millennial favourites, AI-themed painting) can repeat the 2021 cycle before the last one has cleared.
Dealers’ waiting lists and resale clauses hide the true price fall; auction is the visible fraction.
The Bank of America figure of young contemporary 88% below its 2022 peak is in the terminal and was not opened here.
Museum validation is slow and uneven; following institutions means paying up once the show is announced.

record.note: A current artist record, cited as the marker of the segment’s new price level; the 2021–22 records (Boafo, Yukhnovich, Weyant) were not opened.

theses.t: Dealers: flat sales, fairs up, online down
theses.thesis: Dealer sales were $34.8bn in 2025, up 2%, with a third of galleries selling less, online down to 16% of their turnover and fairs up to 35%. The terminal expects the primary market to keep consolidating around fairs and the largest galleries for a decade, which favours buying from estates and from the lists institutions are buying rather than from first shows.

evidence.f: Dealer sales were an estimated $34.8bn in 2025, up 2%; 42% of dealers reported higher sales, 33% lower and 25% stable; dealers above $10m grew 3%, and those under $500,000 saw double-digit rises in average sale values.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Online was 16% of dealer turnover in 2025 (down 6 points) while art fairs rose to 35% of dealer sales from 31%; public auction sales rose 9% but auction houses’ private sales fell 5%.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Artprice (10 March 2026) describes galleries as fragile, with closures and restructuring, and auction houses adapting through revised estimates, more selective offerings and more private sales.
src: Artprice, The Art Market Report 2025 (Spanish edition), 10 Mar 2026

evidence.f: Frieze Seoul 2026 drew 178 museums and institutions from 25 countries, a fair record, and sales of $1m or more by Hauser & Wirth, Almine Rech, Ropac and Pace; David Zwirner’s James Green said ‘the buying power in the region remains strong’.
Regional contrasts: Brazilian galleries’ sales rose 21% in 2025, while 48.4% of Korean galleries and fairs reported lower sales.

risks: Fair costs and mega-gallery concentration squeeze the middle, which is where new artists are first priced.
Gallery closures cut off primary supply for emerging artists and strand their collectors without a market-maker.
UBS flags geopolitical, tariff and cost risks for 2026; a US tariff on art would hit the fair circuit first.
The dealer figures are a survey of respondents, not a census.

record.note: A fair sale, not an auction: the highest price for a Korean artist at Frieze Seoul since its 2022 launch. The date is the fair’s closing day; the report gives a range, as dealers do.

theses.t: Hong Kong holds; Seoul and Tokyo bid
theses.thesis: Hong Kong’s autumn 2026 evening sale rose 35% to HK$739m, its best since 2023, with Asia records for Renoir and Matisse and the most new bidders in 14 years, while Seoul’s auctions rose 16.6% in 2025 and Frieze Seoul drew 178 museums. The terminal expects Hong Kong to remain Asia’s saleroom for twenty years, with Seoul and Tokyo as the fairs where new money is met first.

evidence.f: Sotheby’s Hong Kong Modern and Contemporary evening auction of 28 September 2026 made HK$738.55m (US$96.0m), up 35% on the previous season and the category’s highest Hong Kong total since autumn 2023; Renoir (HK$52.14m) and Matisse (HK$21.03m) set Asia records.
Sotheby’s autumn 2025 Asian Art season drew the highest number of new bidders in 14 years, from 20 regions, and the house transacted over US$346.83m of Asian art worldwide in 2025.

Christie’s Hong Kong 20th/21st Century sales of 26–27 September 2025 made $105.5m, 96% sold by lot, with Picasso’s Buste de femme at $25.4m an Asia record; bidders came from 32 countries and new buyers were 20%.
China’s $8.5bn market (+1%) saw Hong Kong contract in 2025 while the mainland rose; South Korea grew 6% and Japan fell 1%.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

evidence.f: Korean auctions sold 131.5bn won through November 2025 (+16.6%), the first rise in four years, and Frieze Seoul 2026 had 70,000 visitors from 54 countries and 178 museums, its highest figures to date.

risks: Hong Kong carries political and legal risk that New York and London do not; a shock would move the Asian saleroom to Singapore or Tokyo faster than any fair could.
The Asia records are for Western names (Picasso, Renoir, Matisse), which tells where Asian money goes, not that Asian schools are being re-rated.
Tokyo (Art Week Tokyo, Sotheby’s Tokyo), Singapore (Art SG) and Shanghai’s bonded zone were not researched in this session.
Mainland capital controls cap the Hong Kong bid; the 2025 contraction shows it.

record.note: Asia auction record for Picasso; cited as the saleroom marker, not a school record. Sale held 26–27 September 2025.

theses.t: The figure returns: stories outsell surfaces
theses.thesis: The money of 2025–26 has gone to pictures with people in them: Kahlo’s bed, Nara’s child, Ravi Varma’s Yashoda, Binzagr’s coffee shop, Hurvin Anderson’s Last House and the Surrealist collections that sold white-glove. The terminal reads a fifty-year swing back from process and surface to narrative, portraiture and myth, which favours the figurative moderns of every region over the next thirty years.

evidence.f: Sotheby’s three New York sales of 20 November 2025 made $304.5m with fees, all sold; Kahlo’s self-portrait in bed made $54.7m and the 24-lot Surrealist ‘Exquisite Corpus’ collection $98m, with records for Tanning, Bellmer and Paalen.

At Christie’s London on 14 October 2026 Bacon’s Figure in Movement (1978) led at £17.2m with fees and Hurvin Anderson’s Last House (2013) made £5.7m with fees, more than double its £2m low estimate after bidding among three phone bidders.
In Hong Kong on 28 September 2026 two Nara figure paintings made HK$71.66m and HK$61.9m, Ishida’s Can’t Fly Anymore beat its high estimate and the figurative Foujita single-artist sale sold 100%.

Ravi Varma’s mythological Yashoda and Krishna made $17.9m in Mumbai on 1 April 2026; DAG’s Ashish Anand spoke of ‘a growing recognition of mythology as a serious and desirable genre within the global art market’.

The counter-evidence is also strong: Mondrian’s Composition III made £25.2m the same London night, Kusama’s Infinity-Nets beat its estimate in Hong Kong, and a Yuan calligraphy scroll made HK$250m in 2025.

risks: Taste cycles are long but not permanent; abstraction’s top prices (Rothko, Mondrian, Kandinsky) remain above most figurative records.
The figurative boom of 2020–22 in young painting is the segment now down 26.6%; the swing favours proven moderns, not new names.
Surrealism’s run since the 2024 centenary rests on a few single-owner collections.
A ‘fifty-year’ reading cannot be tested on two seasons of data.

record.note: Top lot of the night and the highest figurative price of Hong Kong’s autumn 2026; not Nara’s record.

signals.p: Global art sales were an estimated $59.6bn in 2025, up 4% on 2024 but still 9% below 2023 and under the 2022 peak, on 41.5m transactions (+2%). The US took 44% ($26.0bn, +5%), the UK 18% ($10.5bn, +2%) and China 14% ($8.5bn, +1%); France rose 9% to $4.5bn. The three leaders hold 76% of sales. Public auctions rose 9% in value while the houses’ private sales fell 5%.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

signals.t: The top is back: $10m lots up 40%
signals.p: US fine-art auction lots above $10m rose by nearly 40% in 2025, and 56% of offline fine-art auction value came from lots of $1m or more. Christie’s first-half 2026 auction sales were $3.5bn, up 71% on a year earlier. The strength is concentrated in estates and guaranteed trophies, not in the middle market.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

signals.p: Artprice’s 33rd contemporary report (8 October 2026) counts a 6% rise in contemporary auction value and 9% in volume in the year to 30 June 2026, after three years of decline, with the whole gain of about $100m recorded in the United States. Artists under 40 fell 26.6%. China fell 18%, the Middle East 28%, while France rose 22%. The report says growth returned ‘without higher prices’.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

signals.p: Online-only sales fell to $9.2bn in 2025, 15% of the market (down 3 points) and the lowest since 2019, from a 25% peak in 2020. Online was 16% of dealer turnover while fairs rose to 35% of dealer sales from 31%. Online-only auctions drew just 2% of their value from lots above $1m. The 2021 channel for young art has thinned.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

signals.t: New bidders: younger, and from more places
signals.p: Millennials and Gen Z were 47% of Christie’s new clients in the first half of 2026, and 55% of bidders in its Irsay collection sale were new to the house. At Christie’s Hong Kong in September 2025 new buyers were 20%, more than half of them millennials, from 32 countries. Sotheby’s autumn 2025 Asian Art season drew its highest number of new bidders in 14 years.

Sotheby’s Hong Kong evening auction of 28 September 2026 made HK$738.55m (US$96.0m), up 35% on the previous season and the highest in the category since autumn 2023, with Asia records for Renoir (HK$52.14m) and Matisse (HK$21.03m), a Vietnamese record for Vu Cao Dam (HK$28.96m) and a white-glove Foujita sale (HK$67.2m). Japanese artists sold 100%. The PSYCHO exhibition drew nearly 85,000 visitors in 12 days.

Eight Korean auction houses sold 131.5bn won through November 2025, up 16.6% and the first rise in four years, on 20% fewer lots, with eight works above 1bn won. The market remains far below its 2021 domestic hammer peak of 324.2bn won and the 2022 transaction peak of 806.6bn won. In a December 2025 survey 48.4% of galleries and fairs reported lower sales and 27.1% expect a further fall in 2026.

signals.t: Guarantees carry the evening; the unguaranteed fail
signals.p: All 41 lots of Christie’s Monsoon sale on 14 October 2026 were guaranteed, 11 by the house, and 98% sold; the 20th/21st Century sale that night sold 85%. In May 2025 the unguaranteed $70m Giacometti bust stalled at $64m and was passed, in a Sotheby’s sale where 24 of 26 guaranteed sold lots were backed by third parties. A guarantee moves risk; it does not create a second bidder.

signals.t: The Gulf builds its own season
signals.p: Christie’s held its first Abu Dhabi fine-art sale on 1 November 2026, twenty years after its first Dubai sale, and its chief executive says ‘the market can sustain two centres’. Frieze’s first Abu Dhabi fair follows in November and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens on 11 December 2026. Sotheby’s Origins II in Riyadh made $19.5m in January 2026 with a third of lots to local buyers. Against this, Middle East contemporary auction sales fell 28% in the year to June 2026.
src: Artprice Contemporary Art Market Report 2026, release of 8 Oct 2026 via UNI/PRNewswire

signals.t: Women: 37% of dealer sales and the records
signals.p: Women were 45% of artists represented by dealers in 2025 and 37% of dealer sales by value, both up. Kahlo’s $54.7m on 20 November 2025 set the record for a woman artist, and Christie’s London on 14 October 2026 set records for Popova (£7.6m), Riley (£5.2m) and Hepworth as a painter. The real-terms ceiling is still O’Keeffe’s 2014 price, about $60.5m today.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026 (Arts Economics)

signals.t: India sets its records at home
signals.p: Raja Ravi Varma’s Yashoda and Krishna made $17.9m with fees at Saffronart Mumbai on 1 April 2026, a record for an Indian painting, bought by Cyrus Poonawalla because national-treasure status keeps it in India. Saffronart’s 27 September 2025 sale made Rs 355.77 crore, all 85 lots sold, with a Gaitonde record at Rs 67.08 crore. Christie’s New York’s $27m on 25 March 2026 is the most for a South Asian sale outside India.

signals.t: Scarcity pays: a Yuan scroll and a Rembrandt
signals.p: A Yuan dynasty handscroll by Rao Jie made HK$250m (US$32m) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2025, 25 times its estimate after more than 200 bids, in an Asian works-of-art season worth HK$1.17bn, the most valuable since 2013. In London a re-identified Rembrandt made £6.75m in December 2025 and went to the Leiden Collection, and a Rembrandt drawing made nearly $18m in New York in February 2026. Finite supply, not fashion, set these prices.

unconfirmed: Christie’s Abu Dhabi MAWASIM result of 1 November 2026 ($8.94m, 60 of 68 lots, Monir Farmanfarmaian $844,800) is in the terminal from USA Art News; the results page was not opened in this session.
Yayoi Kusama’s death (reported in search headlines of 27 August 2026, aged 97; the terminal gives 14 August 2026) was not read on an opened page; the effect on her prices is unmeasured.
Zao Wou-Ki’s record (Juin-Octobre 1985, HK$510m, about $65m, Sotheby’s Hong Kong, 30 September 2018) is carried from memory and the brief.
Qi Baishi’s record (Twelve Landscape Screens, RMB 931.5m, Poly Beijing, 17 December 2017) and Giacometti’s L’Homme au doigt ($141.3m, 2015) are the terminal’s entries, not re-opened here.
Leonora Carrington’s $28.5m (Sotheby’s New York, 15 May 2024), Tarsila do Amaral’s and Botero’s records were not opened.
Goncharova’s record and Kabakov’s record (Beetle, Phillips London, 2008) are from memory; Soviet nonconformist prices since 2022 and MacDougall’s current sale calendar were not established.
Kim Whanki’s 2019 record is given by the source as HK$88m (US$11.3m), apparently hammer; the premium price (about HK$102m) and the sale day (23 November 2019) are from memory.
Mehretu’s record day (15 November 2023) and Husain’s Gram Yatra sale day (March 2025) are from memory; the sources give the month only.

Amoako Boafo’s price fall since 2021, Enwonwu’s Tutu in sterling (£1.2m, Bonhams, February 2018), 1-54 and Art X Lagos figures, and Bonhams/Sotheby’s/Christie’s African sale totals were not confirmed (the Artnet page refused).
Gutai (Shiraga, Tanaka), Affandi, Hendra Gunawan and Le Pho records were not researched; Nara’s record (Knife Behind Back, Sotheby’s Hong Kong, 2019) is from memory.
Artprice’s 2025 annual report PDF could not be read, so sculpture’s share of auction turnover and the period shares (Old Masters, Modern, Post-war) are missing.

Hepworth’s sculpture record (Sculpture with Colour (Eos), £6.19m, Christie’s London, 21 October 2026) and the Bank of America figure of young contemporary 88% below its 2022 peak are in the terminal and were not opened here.

The Kiran Nadar Museum of Art’s Adjaye building (announced 2023) has no confirmed opening date here; NMACC and the India Art Fair 2026 were not researched; the count of Indian ‘national treasure’ artists (nine or eleven) is unresolved.
Sotheby’s first Riyadh sale (February 2025, about $17.3m from memory), Art Basel Qatar (February 2026; 87 galleries in the terminal) and the Gulf import and free-port rules were not opened.
Digital and AI art records of 2026 were not researched; no thesis is offered.
Tokyo (Art Week Tokyo, Sotheby’s Tokyo), Singapore (Art SG), Shanghai’s bonded zone and Mumbai as sale rooms were not researched beyond the Indian auction results above.
Jenny Saville’s 2025 National Portrait Gallery show and record, and the Joan Mitchell, Lee Krasner and Agnes Martin records, were not opened.
Poly Auction and China Guardian 2025–26 totals for classical painting and calligraphy were not established; Artpro’s RMB 686m for China Guardian Beijing covers modern and contemporary art only.
Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1923), guaranteed at $60–80m for Christie’s New York on 17 November 2026, is in the terminal and is the next test of the Russian avant-garde thesis; not opened here.
Ownership of the brief’s ‘Chagall’s early work’ within the Russian avant-garde market, and export rules for Russian works, were not researched.

years.note: The pandemic year: Art Basel/UBS (as relayed by CNN) put 2020 public auction sales at about US$17.6bn, down 30%, while online sales doubled to US$12.4bn. The two trophies of the year came from outside the New York system — Wu Bin’s ‘Ten Views of a Lingbi Rock’ (RMB 512.9m, Poly Beijing, October, consigned by an American collector who paid US$1.21m in 1989, fought over by two bidders for nearly an hour) and Sanyu’s ‘Five Nudes’ (HK$304m, Christie’s Hong Kong, July). In January Sotheby’s guaranteed a Tiepolo ‘without the support of a third party’ and, per e-mails later reported, its owner Patrick Drahi ‘picked up the tab’. Sotheby’s own 2020 total was about US$5bn (The Art Newspaper’s prior-year comparison).

years.guaranteed_share: no market-wide share found; the Macklowe sale (US$676.1m) was 100% guaranteed by Sotheby’s, with irrevocable bids on 22 of 35 lots (The Art Newspaper)
years.asia_share: Sotheby’s: Asian clients placed one-third of bids by value in its worldwide auctions and 46% of bids on works over US$5m (The Art Newspaper, December 2021)
years.note: The rebound year. Sotheby’s reached US$7.3bn, the highest in its history, with 39% of buyers new to the house and online sales above US$800m. Divorce and estates fed the top: the court-ordered Macklowe sale (US$588.7m hammer), the Solow estate’s unguaranteed Botticelli (US$80m hammer, seemingly to a Russian client, with an Asian underbidder), and a living collector’s Basquiat ‘In This Case’ (US$81m hammer, three phone bidders). Asian money was visible at the top: Justin Sun took the Macklowe Giacometti through Sotheby’s Hong Kong, and Patti Wong’s phone took the US$82.5m Rothko. The crypto bubble produced Beeple’s US$69.3m NFT, bought by Singapore-based Vignesh Sundaresan through Metapurse. Other lots at US$40m+ found this year but not added: Basquiat ‘Versus Medici’ (US$50.8m, Sotheby’s, 12 May) and Twombly ‘Untitled (Rome)’ (US$41.6m, Sotheby’s, 12 May).

years.note: The year the market turned down while estates kept the top end alive. Sotheby’s sold Emily Fisher Landau’s Picasso ‘Femme à la montre’ (US$139.4m) inside a fully guaranteed 31-lot sale, and in June a family that had owned Klimt’s ‘Dame mit Fächer’ since 1994 sold it in London for £85.3m with a third-party irrevocable bid, to a Hong Kong client of Patti Wong after a ten-minute duel with Sotheby’s own Asia desk. Christie’s full-year total fell to US$6.2bn. Lots at US$40m+ known from memory but not confirmed in this session are listed under ‘unconfirmed’.

years.note: The trough. Christie’s total fell 6% to US$5.7bn, auctions down 16% to US$4.2bn, while private sales rose 41% to US$1.5bn (27% of the total). Only one lot passed US$100m worldwide: Mica Ertegun’s estate Magritte (US$121.2m, 10 minutes of bidding, won by an anonymous collector through Alex Rotter who ‘needed currency conversion’), inside a Christie’s-guaranteed collection that made US$194m across four sales. Sotheby’s sold Sydell Miller’s Monet ‘Nymphéas’ for US$65.5m. At Sotheby’s May Modern sale about two-thirds of the value was pre-sold through house guarantees laid off to irrevocable bidders; Eduardo Costantini bought the Carrington in the room and Jen Hua’s phone took the Monet ‘Meules’. The Apex stegosaurus (US$44.6m) went to Kenneth Griffin.

years.note: The recovery, driven by estates and guarantees. Art Basel/UBS put global sales at US$59.6bn (+4%) and public auctions at US$20.7bn (+9%), with the value of lots over US$10m up 30% and all ten top lots sold in New York. Sotheby’s projected US$7bn (+17%), auctions US$5.7bn (+26%); Christie’s US$6.2bn (+6%), auctions US$4.7bn, private sales US$1.5bn (24%). The Leonard Lauder estate’s 24 lots made US$527.4m with fees, led by the Klimt Lederer portrait (US$205m hammer after nearly 20 minutes, to Julian Dawes’s phone, over four phones and one woman in the room); the Weis collection (US$218m) was all but three lots third-party guaranteed, and the two house-backed lots that failed ‘became property of Christie’s’; the Pritzkers’ Van Gogh went to Patti Wong in the room (US$54m hammer); Basquiat ‘Crowns’ went to an Asian collector through Jen Hua. Sotheby’s Asia chairman Evelyn Lin called Asian participation ‘a defining force’. Other US$40m+ lots found but not added: Monet ‘Nymphéas’ (US$45.4m) and Hockney ‘Christopher Isherwood and Don Bachardy’ (US$44.3m), both Christie’s New York 17 November 2025; the Riggio Mondrian and the Canaletto are in the lot list.

The Newhouse estate’s 16 lots made US$630.8m, fully third-party guaranteed: Pollock ‘Number 7A’ US$157m hammer after two phones duelled from US$107m (Newhouse paid US$32m in 2000); Brancusi US$93m hammer; the Agnes Gund estate’s Rothko set a record at US$85m hammer; Robert Mnuchin’s estate Rothko made US$74m hammer in a fully guaranteed 11-lot sale. In June Sotheby’s London sold the Lewis Collection for £306.6m (Sotheby’s figure), a European single-owner record, and a Monet ‘Nymphéas’ hammered at £40.8m to one of five bidders. In October Peter Simon’s Monsoon collection (£107.5m) and the restituted Lewenstein Kandinsky (£27m hammer, third-party guaranteed, to Maria Los’s Americas phone) led London, and the Schlumberger Monet ‘Iris’ took €50m in Paris after 45 minutes and six bidders. Other US$40m+ lots found in May 2026 but not added: Lichtenstein ‘Anxious Girl’ (US$46m), Twombly ‘Untitled’ 1961 (US$45.4m), Picasso ‘Homme à la guitare’ (US$40.8m), all Christie’s New York 18 May 2026.

Price discrepancies between the terminal and the sources opened: Pollock ‘Number 7A’ (US$181.2m vs The Art Newspaper’s US$181.8m; Art & Object says US$181m); Lewis Collection total (£296.3m vs Sotheby’s £306.6m); Rothko ‘Yellow Stripe’ US$62.2m vs US$62.1m; Lauder Klimt US$236.4m vs US$236.3m.

Two attribution errors in the terminal’s lot list, corrected in the entries: Monet ‘Nymphéas’ US$65.5m was Sotheby’s New York, 18 November 2024, Sydell Miller collection (not Christie’s/Ertegun); Van Gogh ‘Piles de romans parisiens’ US$62.7m was Sotheby’s New York, 20 November 2025, Pritzker collection (not Christie’s, 17 November).

markets.role: The US took US$26.0bn of the US$59.6bn global market in 2025 (44%, up 5%), and all ten of the year’s highest auction prices and 39 of the top 50 were made in New York (Art Basel & UBS report, 2026). sothebys, christies and phillips run the May and November marquee weeks; Klimt’s ‘Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer’ made US$236.3m at Sotheby’s in November 2025. The dealers’ Chelsea–Tribeca–Upper East Side triangle is thinning: zwirner is leaving East 69th Street, pace cut staff in June 2026, blum and olneygleason mark the 2025 shake-out. Lending concentrates here (sfs, bofa, citi, jpmorgan, athena), storage in uovo, crozier and arcis, with delawarefreeport as the sales-tax escape. Sales tax 8.875% (from memory).

markets.role: Second market: the UK made US$10.5bn in 2025, an 18% share, up 2% (Art Basel & UBS, 2026). christies, sothebys, phillips and bonhams hold the March, June and October weeks; Sotheby’s Pauline Karpidas sale made US$137m and Christie’s Canaletto £31.9m in 2025. Frieze London and Frieze Masters changed hands in May 2025, sold by Endeavor to Ari Emanuel’s new events company for a reported US$200m, with Simon Fox staying as chief executive (The Art Newspaper, 1 May 2025). Mayfair is contracting: gagosian left Burlington Arcade in July 2026 and pace wants something smaller than Hanover Square. The service layer is here: advisers fineartgroup, gurrjohns and npap, insurers hiscox and lloyds, shipper momart. Import VAT on art 5% (from memory).

markets.role: France made US$4.5bn in 2025, up 9%, an 8% share (Art Basel & UBS, 2026); Paris October auctions rose 30% year on year and Art Basel Paris at the Grand Palais has held the October slot since 2022 (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025). christies and sothebys on avenue Matignon, artcurial at the Rond-Point, tajan and the drouot cooperative’s rooms share the calendar. Dealers cluster in the Marais (ropac, crousel, perrotin, templon, hetzler) and on avenue Matignon (whitecube, alminerech, skarstedt, perrotin, which reopened 8 avenue Matignon in April 2025), with Ropac’s Pantin halls and gagosian at Le Bourget beside the airport. France cut VAT on art in 2025 (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025); the 5.5% rate is from memory.

The Art Newspaper, Art market 2025 review, 19 Dec 2025

markets.role: Asia’s sale room, still below its 2021 peak. Christie’s Asia auction sales fell 5% in 2025 and Asia Pacific buyer spend 3% (SCMP, Dec 2025); christies trades from The Henderson under Rahul Kadakia, President Asia Pacific from January 2026, sothebys from Landmark Chater under Masumi Shinohara, phillips from West Kowloon; guardian, poly and bonhams hold spring and autumn sales. Art Basel Hong Kong (HKCEC, 27–29 March 2026) drew 91,500 visitors and whitecube reported about £5m of sales (Art Basel, March 2026). The dealer footprint is thinning (pace closed its space in 2025) while gagosian, zwirner, hauserwirth, whitecube, perrotin, massimodecarlo, benbrown and tang stay in Central. No VAT, sales tax or import duty on art (from memory).

markets.role: The trade’s back office, not a market. Ports Francs et Entrepôts de Genève SA (genevafreeport), majority-owned by the Canton of Geneva, made CHF 23.797m of revenue and CHF 1.170m net profit in 2025; a new 14,500 m² art-storage building at La Praille, fully let for 15 years, is due in early 2028 (annual report 2025; chairman Sylvain Matthey-Junod, director general Martin Leslie Dunning). Switzerland’s art sales rose 13% in 2025 (Art Basel & UBS, 2026). The rooms sell jewels and watches: sothebys and christies in May and November, phillips with Bacs & Russo. ubs and the swissbanks lend without publishing figures; koller and hauserwirth (two Zurich galleries) lead Zurich; nahmad’s inventory is reported to sit in the freeport (from memory).

markets.role: A fair town with a thin permanent layer. Art Basel in Basel (18–21 June 2026) brought 290 galleries from 43 countries and 90,000 visitors; hauserwirth reported Picasso’s ‘Le peintre et son modèle dans un paysage’ (1963) sold at an asking price of US$35m (Art Basel, June 2026; director Maike Cruse). The owner MCH Group (James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems as anchor shareholder since 2020, from memory) calls Doha its fifth fair after Basel, Miami Beach, Hong Kong and Paris (Art Basel, May 2025). Year-round: hauserwirth’s Basel gallery and publishers, the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen, artcurial’s Beurret Bailly Widmer arm, and gagosian’s Rheinsprung 1, which it is leaving after 17 shows since 2019 (The Art Newspaper, 31 July 2026).

markets.role: Mainland China was the third market in 2025 at US$8.5bn, a 14% share, up just over 1% (Art Basel & UBS, 2026). Beijing is the auction capital: guardian (Taikang-controlled) and state-backed poly hold the spring and autumn sales, with yongle the challenger since 2020 (from memory); christies keeps a Shanghai office and the foreign houses sell through Hong Kong. Shanghai is the gallery and fair city: shanghart at West Bund, lisson, perrotin and alminerech, continua and tang in Beijing’s 798, and the November pairing of West Bund Art & Design and ART021 (from memory). Mainland import VAT and duty keep bonded stock and the big sales in Hong Kong (from memory).

markets.role: The Asian market that grew in 2025: South Korea up 6% (Art Basel & UBS, 2026), and Korean auction sales nearly doubled year on year in the first half of 2026 on a few very high-value lots (Korea Art Authentication and Appraisal Institute, cited by The Art Newspaper, 3 Sept 2026). Frieze Seoul (fifth year, director Patrick Lee) and Kiaf run together in early September; kukje sold a 1971 Yoo Youngkuk for KRW 2.2–2.5bn (about US$1.6–1.8m) and ropac a Ghenie at €1.1m (The Art Newspaper, 3 Sept 2026). seoulauction and kauction are the houses; kukje and hyundai the local powers; pace, ropac, whitecube, perrotin, lehmannmaupin, gladstone, estherschipper and tang have Seoul galleries.

markets.role: A hub, not a sale room. ART SG (22–25 January 2026, Marina Bay Sands) drew over 43,000 visitors, with more than 100 exhibitors from over 30 countries alongside S.E.A. Focus; Magnus Renfrew is co-founder and Shuyin Yang fair director, UBS the founding partner (ART SG, Jan 2026). The fair belongs to The Art Assembly, formed in 2022 by Sandy Angus, Tim Etchells and Renfrew with Taipei Dangdai, India Art Fair, Sydney Contemporary and PHOTOFAIRS Shanghai (ART SG, April 2022). Le Freeport beside Changi (sgfreeport) passed from Yves Bouvier to Jihan Wu for a reported US$28.4m in 2022 (The Art Newspaper); helutrans runs the bonded galleries at Tanjong Pagar (from memory). No house holds regular sales here; GST 9% (from memory).

markets.role: Japan’s market slipped 1% in 2025 (Art Basel & UBS, 2026), and the dealers’ picture is mixed: pace opened at Azabudai Hills Garden Plaza A and perrotin keeps a Tokyo gallery (Ocula), while blum, the gallery that took Nara and Murakami to America, announced in July 2025 that its Tokyo and Los Angeles spaces would close (The Art Newspaper). takaishii is the local gallery of record and sbiart the domestic contemporary auctioneer (from memory); christies, sothebys and phillips keep offices, not sale rooms. Tokyo Gendai, The Art Assembly’s fair at Pacifico Yokohama each July since 2023, is the market’s fair (from memory). A 10% consumption tax applies to sales and imports (from memory).

markets.role: The Gulf’s commercial hub: DIFC for the houses and Alserkal Avenue for the galleries. sothebys and christies keep DIFC offices and sale rooms; perrotin opened a 1,100 m² DIFC gallery on 16 April 2025 beside them, its second attempt after a 2022–23 space (Ocula, April 2025). Alserkal holds leilaheller, custot and thirdline (locations from memory); continua sits in the Burj Khalifa (from memory). Art Dubai in March added two director roles in 2025 (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025) and the western slump is pushing galleries to the Gulf (Al-Monitor, Feb 2026). VAT 5%, no income tax (from memory); falcon’s parent group is based here. The one number: Perrotin’s 1,100 m² (April 2025).

markets.role: The sovereign money. ADQ, the emirate’s fund, put US$1bn into sothebys in 2024; Sotheby’s first Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week made US$133.4m in December 2025 (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025). Frieze replaces Abu Dhabi Art with Frieze Abu Dhabi, established with the Department of Culture and Tourism: 19–22 November 2026 at Manarat Al Saadiyat, more than 80 galleries from 37 countries, director Dyala Nusseibeh, with gagosian, pace, perrotin, leilaheller, custot, thirdline, athr and naturemorte taking part and Deutsche Bank (deutsche) as lead partner (Frieze, 2026); the fair had not yet opened on 12 November 2026. Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi project anchor Saadiyat; the 2021 plan committed US$6bn to culture over five years (Al-Monitor, Feb 2026).

markets.role: The newest sale room. sothebys held its second Diriyah auction, ‘Origins II’, on 31 January 2026 at Bujaira Terrace: US$15.4m hammer, US$19.5m with fees, 89% sold by lot, about a third of buyers Saudi; Safeya Binzagr’s ‘Coffee Shop in Madina Road’ (1968) made US$2.1m, a record for a Saudi artist (The Art Newspaper, 3 Feb 2026). The first sale, February 2025, made US$17.2m from 140 lots at 67% sold. athr (Jeddah, Riyadh, AlUla) is the local gallery; colnaghi plans a Riyadh space backed by a Saudi firm (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025). Cultural investment is put at more than US$21.6bn since 2016 (Al-Monitor, Feb 2026), though PIF cutbacks were reported in early 2026. Auction-licence and import rules were not established.

Art Basel Qatar debuted in February 2026 at the M7 hub and Doha Design District in Msheireb, a partnership of MCH Group, Qatar Sports Investments and QC+ (Art Basel, May 2025), with 87 galleries, more than half from the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia (The Art Newspaper, Dec 2025). markets.role: India’s auction turnover hit a decade high of ₹2,543 crore in 2025, with 4,057 of 5,059 lots sold (360 ONE data via Business Today, Sept 2026). saffronart made US$40.2m in New Delhi on 27 September 2025, the largest sale in South Asia, and sold Raja Ravi Varma’s ‘Yashoda and Krishna’ for ₹167.2 crore in Mumbai in April 2026; astaguru and pundoles sell in Mumbai, dag deals from inventory. Christie’s and Sotheby’s sell South Asian art in New York and London, not India (Husain US$13.7m, Christie’s, March 2025). vadehra, chemould and naturemorte are the galleries; India Art Fair (The Art Assembly) is Delhi’s February fixture. GST on art was cut from 12% to 5% in September 2025 (The Art Newspaper, Oct 2025).

markets.role: West Africa’s market is one fair and a handful of galleries; none is in the players file. ART X Lagos, founded by Tokini Peterside-Schwebig in 2016, held its tenth edition on 6–9 November 2025 at the Federal Palace Hotel with 15 exhibitors, 11 from Lagos, down from nearly twice as many before 2023; it draws 10,000–12,000 visitors a year, and kó is among the exhibitors (The Art Newspaper, 4 Nov 2025). The naira crisis and soft demand for African art abroad shape prices; the founder cited a strengthening naira as grounds for optimism. Arthouse Contemporary runs the local auctions; Rele and SMO Contemporary are the other galleries (from memory). No international house or mega-gallery has a Lagos space.

markets.role: Latin America’s largest market by fair. SP-Arte’s 22nd edition (8–12 April 2026, Niemeyer’s biennial pavilion in Ibirapuera, founder Fernanda Feitosa) brought more than 180 galleries, design studios and institutions, with the design sector grown from 23 to 64 stands since 2016; Brazilian galleries’ sales rose 21% in 2025 (Art Basel & UBS report, cited by The Art Newspaper, 10 April 2026). mendeswood and nararoesler are the exporters, with Brussels, New York and Paris spaces; bolsadearte is the auctioneer; Inhotim and the Pinacoteca anchor the institutions. ArtRio follows in September (from memory). Import duties and customs rules remain the market’s brake (from memory). Brazil’s market size is not broken out in the UBS report, and no attendance figure was given.

markets.role: Zona Maco, in its 24th year at Centro Banamex (to 8 February 2026), is Latin America’s foremost fair and now shares its week with Art Basel Qatar; organisers listed more than 75 visiting museum groups, largely from the US and Canada, and pace sold nearly its whole Kylie Manning stand at the VIP preview (The Art Newspaper, 6 Feb 2026). kurimanzutto and omr are the international galleries, Proyectos Monclova and the 90-year-old Galería de Arte Mexicano the local establishment, morton the auction house, Museo Jumex and the Soumaya the collectors’ museums. Material and Salón Acme are the satellite fairs (from memory). No foreign house holds sales in Mexico; VAT is 16% (from memory).

law_more.method: Research of 9 Nov 2026 within a budget of 25 searches and 40 fetches, spent first on Bangladesh, Canada and the capital-control pages. Primary pages opened: Bangladesh FERA 1947 (law-firm mirror of the Act); Canada Cultural Property Export and Import Act s.4, Control List Group V, Canadian Heritage permit page, CBSA Customs Tariff ch. 97 (2025), FINTRAC EFT guidance, Canada Gazette SOR/2022-102; HCCH Apostille status table; PwC Nigeria on the 2022 Act; EY and Marval on the BCRA communications; Bank BCA on BI thresholds; LuatVietnam on Circular 20/2022; FATF Feb 2023 report; FinCEN 2022 alert; OFSI 2025 threat assessment. Where no page was opened the cell is carried from memory and marked U; the terminal should show those cells as unverified. Field names follow v24 law_world.json, plus ‘treasure’, ‘special’ and the new ‘capital’ block. vf: V = primary; S = secondary; U = memory or weak page.

export.law: Antiquities Act 1968 (as amended 1976): no antiquity may be exported without a licence from the Director General of Archaeology; the Act reaches objects of historical or artistic interest and the Government may declare any object an antiquity. No export licence is known for a contemporary painting or sculpture (U).
export.needs: An export declaration through the customs system; for anything the Department of Archaeology might treat as an antiquity, its licence or a no-objection letter. Not opened on an official page this session (U).
export.authority: Department of Archaeology, Ministry of Cultural Affairs; Bangladesh Customs (National Board of Revenue).
export.temporary: Bangladesh is not in the ATA carnet chain (from memory, U); temporary exports move on an ordinary customs bond.
export.treasure: Found antiquities belong to the State under the 1968 Act (U).
export.note: No Bangladesh heritage or customs page opened this session; the budget went to the exchange-control law. Everything here is from memory.

import.duty: Chapter 97 attracts customs duty under Bangladesh’s tariff (rate not confirmed; 25% ad valorem on 9701 recalled, U) plus the usual supplementary and advance taxes.
import.overlays: Advance income tax and advance trade VAT are collected at import on most goods (U).
import.vat: 15% standard VAT, charged on import (U).
import.special: No reduced rate or art-specific relief found (U).
import.cpia: Bangladesh is a party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention (U).

aml.rule: Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 (amended 2015), supervised by the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit. Reporting organisations are banks, financial institutions, insurers, money changers, remitters, dealers in precious metals and stones, real-estate developers, lawyers, accountants and NGOs; art dealers and auctioneers are not listed (U). The 2022 overseas-investment rules state that misuse of an approved investment ‘will be treated as money laundering’ (press report).
aml.threshold: Cash transaction reports above BDT 1,000,000 (10 lakh) in a day (U).
aml.asks: Banks ask for national ID, the source of funds and the purpose of any outward remittance; authorised dealers submit remittance applications to Bangladesh Bank (U).
src: Prothom Alo, Bangladesh allows local firms to make overseas equity investment, 27 Jan 2022
aml.note: The Act and the BFIU circulars were not opened.

sanctions.rule: Bangladesh applies the UN Security Council lists through the Anti-Terrorism Act 2009 and BFIU circulars; it has no autonomous sanctions on Russia (U).
sanctions.note: No page opened for this cell this session; carried from memory.

apostille.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Consular and Welfare Wing), Dhaka — from memory (U).
apostille.docs: Bangladesh acceded on 29 Jul 2024; the Convention entered into force for it on 30 Mar 2025 (accession marked A**, so it operates only with Contracting Parties that did not object). Documents for a sale abroad (powers of attorney, notarised provenance affidavits, company papers) are apostilled rather than legalised at the consulate.
src: HCCH status table, Apostille Convention (read 9 Nov 2026; 130 Contracting Parties)

cites.rule: Party to CITES since 1982; the Wildlife (Conservation and Security) Act 2012 bans trade in ivory and listed species products; CITES permits are issued by the Forest Department (U).
cites.note: No page opened for this cell this session; carried from memory.

freeport.rule: No art freeport. Bonded warehouses serve export industries only (U).

capital.rule: Exchange control rests on the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 (FERA, last amended by Act XVII of 2015). s.4(1): nobody but an authorised dealer may buy, borrow, sell, lend or exchange foreign exchange without Bangladesh Bank’s general or special permission; s.4(5) lets a resident buy foreign exchange from an authorised dealer only for a current-account transaction; s.4(6) lets Bangladesh Bank specify which capital-account transactions are permissible. s.5(1): a resident may not make any payment to or for the credit of a person resident outside Bangladesh without Bangladesh Bank’s exemption. s.8(2): taking foreign exchange, gold or jewellery out of the country needs permission. s.19(1) lets the Government or the Bank require residents to repatriate foreign exchange, foreign securities and foreign property. s.23: up to seven years’ imprisonment, a fine and confiscation. A resident is anyone in Bangladesh six months of the last twelve (s.2(hhh)). Buying a work of art abroad with one’s own money is a capital-account transaction for which no general permission was found; it would need Bangladesh Bank’s special permission, and this session found no published route for a resident individual. A non-resident buyer who paid from abroad can repatriate sale proceeds through an authorised dealer against the record of the inward remittance (Form C for inward remittances of US$2,000 or more, 2009 guidelines).
capital.limits: Overseas equity investment: only exporters, from their Export Retention Quota accounts, up to 20% of the firm’s average annual export earnings over five years or under 25% of net assets in the latest audited accounts, approved by a 15-member committee chaired by the Bangladesh Bank governor under the Capital Account Transaction (Overseas Equity Investment) Rules 2022 (issued 9 Jan 2022; the press report cites s.26 of FERA, the Act text opened puts rule-making in s.27 and permissible capital transactions in s.4(6)). Returns must be remitted home within 30 days; misuse is treated as money laundering. Personal purposes: the 2009 guidelines allowed travellers cash and travellers’ cheques of up to US$1,000 equivalent from money changers (US$200 without a visa) within an annual travel quota; press headlines of 2025 report the annual private travel quota raised to US$18,000 and a master circular of 30 Sept consolidating outward-remittance rules for travel, private transfers, dividends, institutional payments and international cards (figures not read on the circular itself, U). Companies may remit US$30,000 a year for an overseas office (2009 guidelines).
capital.routes: An exporter’s approved overseas equity investment from its ERQ; a non-resident investor’s funds brought in and recorded (Form C; non-resident Taka and NITA accounts; sale proceeds of listed securities remittable without prior approval at the day’s market price, unlisted shares with prior approval on audited net asset value; dividends on an auditor-certified form after non-resident tax); inheritance and gifts are not a route for a resident to export capital. There is no lawful route for a resident individual to wire a sum abroad to buy a work of art; the lawful transformation starts only with funds that are already outside Bangladesh with permission or that belong to a non-resident.
