export.law: Cultural Property Export and Import Act, RSC 1985 c. C-51, and the Canadian Cultural Property Export Control List (CRC c. 448). An export permit is needed for any object on the Control List that is 50 years old or more and whose maker is no longer living (s.4(3) of the Act bars listing anything under 50 years old or made by a living person), whatever the reason for export, whether permanent or temporary, and however long it has been in Canada.
export.needs: Group V (fine art) thresholds by fair market value in Canada: made by a person who at any time ordinarily resided in Canada — drawings and prints over C$5,000, paintings and sculptures over C$15,000, other media over C$5,000; Canadian-connected works (commissioned by a Canadian resident, Canadian theme, or tied to a prominent Canadian person, institution or event) — over C$7,500 / C$20,000 / C$7,500; works made outside Canada with no such connection — drawings and prints over C$15,000, paintings and sculptures over C$30,000, other media over C$20,000. Photographs fall under Group VII. Below the thresholds, or for a living artist, nothing but the shipper’s export declaration.
export.authority: CBSA permit-issuing offices issue permanent and temporary permits; an expert examiner reviews permanent applications; general permits come from the Minister of Canadian Heritage (Movable Cultural Property Program); the Canadian Cultural Property Export Review Board hears appeals.
export.fee: No fee is stated on the Canadian Heritage page (U whether it is free).
export.time: Not stated. If a permanent permit is refused and the Review Board upholds the refusal it sets a delay of two to six months during which designated Canadian institutions may buy the object; without an appeal a new application can be made only after two years. The Board can determine a fair cash offer.
export.temporary: Temporary permits (exhibition, conservation, research) are granted automatically; the object must return within five years and a notice of return is due within 15 days.
export.treasure: Objects recovered from Canadian soil, territorial sea or inland waters may be listed at any value (s.4(2)(a)); the Act is a heritage-retention regime, not a treasure-trove regime.
src: Cultural Property Export and Import Act, s.4 (justice.laws.gc.ca)
Canadian Cultural Property Export Control List, Group V Objects of Fine Art
Canadian Heritage, Cultural property export permits (modified 13 Jan 2023)
export.note: Exporting controlled property without a permit is a criminal offence (fines, imprisonment or both).

import.duty: Customs Tariff chapter 97 (T2025): paintings, drawings and pastels, original prints, original sculpture, collectors’ pieces and antiques over 100 years are ‘Free’ at the MFN rate and under all 21 preferential agreements where they are originals by artists; the ‘other’ lines for hand-painted or decorated work that is not an original by an artist carry 5.5% (paintings) and 7% (mosaics, other works) MFN, Free under the agreements. Chapter notes exclude mass-produced reproductions and works of conventional commercial craftsmanship.
import.overlays: Canada’s 2025–26 counter-tariffs on US goods and the US tariffs on Canadian goods were not checked for chapter 97 this session (U). Russian-origin luxury goods: the import ban in Schedule 6 Part 2 does not cover art (see sanctions).
import.vat: 5% GST is collected by CBSA on the value for duty at import; HST or provincial sales tax follows where the work is delivered or for commercial importers’ accounts (from memory, U).
import.state_tax: Provincial HST/PST at the place of delivery (Ontario 13% HST, Quebec 9.975% QST plus GST, Alberta GST only) — from memory (U).
import.special: Works imported for a public institution or museum may be relieved under tariff item 9812 and the Cultural Property Export and Import Act donation route (U).
import.cpia: Under s.37 of the Cultural Property Export and Import Act Canada bars the import of foreign cultural property illegally exported from a reciprocating state (1970 UNESCO Convention) — from memory (U).
src: CBSA, Customs Tariff 2025, Chapter 97 (archived page, issued 1 Jan 2025)
import.note: Duty rates read on the CBSA 2025 tariff (the 2026 tariff not opened); GST/HST at import carried from memory.

aml.rule: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act. Reporting entities that must file electronic funds transfer reports with FINTRAC: financial entities, money services businesses and foreign MSBs, casinos, life insurers (when they offer loans or prepaid products) and, from 1 Jul 2024, armoured-car businesses. Dealers in art and auction houses are not named as reporting entities on the FINTRAC guidance opened; dealers in precious metals and stones are a sector under the Act (from memory, U), and a Toronto sale room is therefore outside FINTRAC while the bank that receives its wire is inside.
aml.threshold: International EFTs of C$10,000 or more (single transaction, or two or more in a static 24-hour window known to share a requester, third party or beneficiary; SWIFT and non-SWIFT aggregated) are reported within 5 business days of initiation or final receipt; domestic transfers are not reported. Foreign currency converted at the Bank of Canada rate on the day. Large cash transactions of C$10,000 or more are reported on the same footing (from memory, U).
aml.asks: The EFT report carries requester, beneficiary, third-party, account-holder, initiator and receiver names, addresses and identifiers, and source-of-funds fields (how the funds were obtained). The receiving bank in Toronto therefore files the name of the Geneva or Dhaka sender and of the beneficiary on every qualifying wire.
src: FINTRAC, Reporting electronic funds transfers to FINTRAC (issued 29 Feb 2024, modified 24 Jun 2024)
aml.note: Large Cash Transaction Reports and the full sector list not opened this session.

sanctions.rule: Special Economic Measures (Russia) Regulations as amended by SOR/2022-102 (registered 18 May 2022, published 8 Jun 2022, luxury-goods bans effective 60 days after coming into force): s.3.8(1) bars any person in Canada or Canadian abroad from exporting, selling, supplying or shipping Schedule 6 Part 1 luxury goods to Russia or anyone in Russia; items 239–257 cover HS 97.01–97.06 — paintings, drawings and pastels, original prints, original sculpture, collages, stamps, collectors’ pieces and antiques, split by age (100 and 250 years), with no value threshold. The import ban (s.3.8(3), Schedule 6 Part 2) covers fish, seafood, caviar, alcohol and diamonds, not art. Personal effects for the traveller’s own use are exempt. s.5 bars facilitation. Penalties under s.8 SEMA: summary up to C$25,000 and/or one year; indictment up to five years. RCMP and CBSA enforce. Dealing prohibitions with the listed persons in Schedule 1 apply to any sale (from memory, U).
src: Canada Gazette Part II, SOR/2022-102, 8 Jun 2022

cites.rule: Party to CITES; the Wild Animal and Plant Protection and Regulation of International and Interprovincial Trade Act (WAPPRIITA) requires permits from Environment and Climate Change Canada for ivory, tortoiseshell and other listed material in a work; Canada banned elephant-ivory and rhino-horn trade in Jan 2024 (from memory, U).

freeport.rule: No art freeport. Bonded warehouses and the CBSA’s customs bonded warehouse programme defer duty (nil for art) and GST until release (U).

capital.rule: No exchange control. A resident may move any sum abroad to buy a work of art and a non-resident may repatriate sale proceeds freely; the controls are reporting, not permission: the bank files an EFT report with FINTRAC for international transfers of C$10,000 or more; the Canada Revenue Agency receives the same international EFT data under the Income Tax Act (from memory, U); foreign property costing over C$100,000 is reported on form T1135 (from memory, U). A cash sum arriving from Dhaka is therefore lawful in Toronto only if it left Bangladesh with Bangladesh Bank’s permission; the Canadian bank will ask for the source of funds and file the EFT report, and if the story does not hold it files a suspicious transaction report.
capital.limits: No limits. Reporting at C$10,000 (EFT, large cash) within 5 business days; no threshold for a suspicious transaction report.
capital.routes: Any lawful route through a financial entity; the bank’s own KYC and source-of-funds questions apply. A loan from a Canadian bank against a work stored in Geneva is possible in principle, with the collateral’s title, appraisal and insurance papers (U).

export.law: Law 24,633 of 1996 on the international circulation of works of art (regulated by Decree 1321/97) and Law 25,197 on the register of cultural heritage: works by living artists, or by artists dead less than 50 years, leave freely on a sworn declaration (‘licencia de exportación’ issued by the Ministry of Culture’s Dirección Nacional de Bienes y Sitios Culturales); older works need the Ministry’s authorisation, which it may refuse for heritage of national interest; archaeological and palaeontological objects are barred under Law 25,743 (2003). All from memory (U).
export.needs: The export licence or sworn declaration, a photograph and description of the work, and the customs export declaration (U).
export.authority: Ministerio de Cultura (Dirección Nacional de Bienes y Sitios Culturales); Dirección General de Aduanas (ARCA, formerly AFIP).
export.temporary: Argentina accepts ATA carnets (Cámara Argentina de Comercio is the guaranteeing body) — from memory (U).
export.treasure: Archaeological and palaeontological finds belong to the State (Law 25,743) (U).
export.note: No Argentine heritage or customs page opened this session.

import.duty: Law 24,633 sets the import duty on works of art at 0% and exempts them from the statistics tax (from memory, U).
import.overlays: Argentina’s ‘PAIS’ tax on foreign-currency purchases lapsed in Dec 2024 and the 30% ‘percepción’ on individuals’ foreign-currency purchases was eliminated by ARCA General Resolution 5672/2025 in Apr 2025 (EY).
import.vat: 21% VAT applies at import (U).
import.state_tax: Gross-receipts taxes at provincial level on dealers, not on the importer (U).
import.special: Works imported for public museums or exhibitions are relieved (U).
import.cpia: Argentina is a party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention (U).

capital.rule: The ‘cepo’ for individuals ended on 14 Apr 2025: BCRA Communication ‘A’ 8226 (11 Apr 2025) gives individuals access to the official exchange market to buy foreign currency without prior BCRA authorisation (the US$200 monthly cap of 2019 is gone) and ARCA Resolution 5672/2025 removed the 30% withholding on those purchases; Decree 269/2025 repealed the 80/20 export-settlement split. Companies still cannot buy foreign currency to hold; they may pay dividends abroad only from earnings of fiscal years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2025, pay imports without the former 30-day wait, pay unrelated-party services on accrual and related-party services after 90 days. Communications ‘A’ 8330 and 8331 (18 Sept 2025) removed the US$36,000 annual limit for individuals keeping service-export proceeds in foreign currency, barred bank commissions on inflows to residents and let non-residents access the market to repatriate direct investments made to buy local companies. A resident individual may therefore buy dollars and wire them abroad to buy a work of art; the bank still applies AML checks and the cross-restriction with securities (90-day ‘parking’) and sworn statements carried from memory (U). Non-residents repatriating portfolio investments or sale proceeds: subject to BCRA rules and minimum holding periods not opened this session (U).
capital.limits: Individuals: no quantitative limit since 14 Apr 2025 (EY; Marval). Companies: no purchase for hoarding; dividends only from 2025 earnings (EY). Export proceeds for certain fuels: 180 days to settle (Marval).
capital.routes: An individual’s own purchase of foreign currency in the official market and transfer abroad; a non-resident’s repatriation of a direct investment under ‘A’ 8331; documented export earnings. Press of Nov 2025 reported the government’s intention to lift the remaining corporate restrictions ‘soon’ (headline only, not opened, U); as of 9 Nov 2026 no later communication was read.

export.law: Antiquities Protection Law 117 of 1983 (amended by Laws 3/2010 and 91/2018): antiquities (objects of 100 years or more of archaeological, artistic or historical value) are State property and may not be exported; trading in them is a crime. Works of art under 100 years old leave with a certificate from the Ministry of Culture (Fine Arts Sector) that the object is not an antiquity, which customs demands for paintings and sculpture — from memory (U).
export.needs: Ministry of Culture / Supreme Council of Antiquities clearance that the object is not an antiquity; customs export declaration (U).
export.authority: Supreme Council of Antiquities (Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities); Ministry of Culture Fine Arts Sector; Egyptian Customs Authority.
export.temporary: Egypt is not an ATA carnet country (U); temporary export of antiquities for exhibition needs a Cabinet-level decision under Law 117 (U).
export.treasure: All antiquities found on or in Egyptian land belong to the State (Law 117 art. 6) (U).

capital.rule: Formal controls were dismantled in 2017: the US$100,000 annual cap on individuals’ foreign-currency transfers abroad imposed after 2011 was lifted in June 2017, and on 28 Nov 2017 the Central Bank of Egypt removed the 2015 caps on importers’ cash deposits (US$10,000 a day, US$50,000 a month) and withdrawals (US$30,000), described as its ‘last remaining official foreign-currency controls’. In the dollar shortage of 2022–Mar 2024 banks rationed foreign currency informally, capped card spending abroad and queued transfers; the 6 Mar 2024 flotation and the IMF and Ras El-Hekma inflows cleared the backlog (from memory, U). As of 2026 a resident may buy foreign currency from a bank and transfer it abroad for a documented purpose, subject to the bank’s AML checks and the CBE’s instructions on the purpose of transfer; the current instructions were not opened (U). Non-residents and foreign investors may repatriate capital, profits and sale proceeds in foreign currency under the Investment Law 72 of 2017, through the bank that recorded the inflow (U).
capital.limits: No published quantitative limit found since 2017; banks apply their own card and transfer ceilings (U).
capital.routes: Documented purchase through a bank; a non-resident’s own funds recorded on arrival; inheritance and gifts through a bank with documents (U).

export.law: National Commission for Museums and Monuments Act (Decree 77 of 1979, Cap N19 LFN 2004): no antiquity may be exported without a permit from the Commission; ‘antiquity’ covers objects made before 1918 and ethnographic objects used in traditional ceremonies. Contemporary art needs the Commission’s export certificate confirming the object is not an antiquity, which customs asks for — from memory (U).
export.needs: NCMM export permit or non-antiquity certificate; Nigeria Customs Service export declaration (U).
export.authority: National Commission for Museums and Monuments; Nigeria Customs Service.
export.temporary: Nigeria is not in the ATA carnet chain (U).
export.treasure: Antiquities discovered are notified to the Commission, which may acquire them (U).

aml.rule: Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (assented 13 May 2022, repealing the 2011 Act). Cash payments above N5,000,000 (individuals) and N10,000,000 (bodies corporate) are prohibited except through a financial institution; transactions above those sums are disclosed; transfers to or from abroad above US$10,000 are reported to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (and the SEC); cash or negotiable instruments above US$10,000 are declared to the Nigeria Customs Service. Designated non-financial businesses are supervised by the Special Control Unit against Money Laundering (SCUML), which may suspend a licence and fine up to N1,000,000; the Act’s DNFBP list includes dealers in jewellery, cars and luxury goods, precious metals and stones, real estate, hotels, casinos and supermarkets (list from memory, U) — an art dealer registers with SCUML as a dealer in luxury goods in practice (U). Nigeria was removed from the FATF grey list in Oct 2025 (from memory, U).
aml.threshold: N5,000,000 (individuals) and N10,000,000 (corporate) for cash; US$10,000 for international transfers and cash declarations.
aml.asks: Bank verification number, ID, source of funds, SCUML registration certificate for DNFBP accounts (U).

capital.rule: Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1995 and the CBN Foreign Exchange Manual: residents may hold domiciliary accounts and buy foreign exchange from banks for ‘invisible’ transactions on Form A (travel, education, medical, subscriptions) within documented limits; a transfer abroad to buy an asset for investment is a capital transaction that needs CBN approval through the bank, and the CBN has since 2015 excluded a list of items from the official window (from memory, U). Since the June 2023 unification and the 2024–25 reforms banks sell foreign currency at market rates, but the documentary rules stand (U). A non-resident who brought capital in through a bank with a Certificate of Capital Importation (CCI) may repatriate capital, dividends and sale proceeds through the same bank at the market rate (U). The 2022 Act adds the US$10,000 international-transfer report to the NFIU and the cash declaration at the border (PwC).

Contemporary art leaves on a customs export declaration, often with a Department of Archaeology certificate that the object is not an antiquity — from memory (U).

capital.rule: Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 (Pakistan’s own, the same 1947 statute as Bangladesh’s) and the State Bank of Pakistan’s Foreign Exchange Manual: a resident may not transfer capital abroad or acquire foreign assets without SBP permission through an authorised dealer; the manual lists the permitted current-account remittances. SBP’s 2021 liberalisation (press report, date on the page not shown) let resident individuals invest in listed securities abroad without approval up to US$25,000 per calendar year (holding under 1% of the investee), employees of foreign-owned subsidiaries remit up to US$50,000 a year into parent share plans, export firms set up offices abroad with up to 10% of three-year average export earnings or US$100,000, and start-ups form holding companies abroad; ‘residents would need to approach SBP for approval through their banks as per existing policy’ for everything else. Buying a work of art abroad is not within any of these windows and needs SBP’s approval (U). Exchange companies’ sales of foreign currency to individuals are capped by SBP (a US$100,000 per person per year ceiling appears in a 2023 Business Recorder headline not opened, U). Non-residents repatriate registered investment and its proceeds through the bank that recorded it; Roshan Digital Accounts give non-resident Pakistanis full repatriability (U).

dhaka_toronto_case.n: Cash in Dhaka → a sale room → the Geneva freeport → a bank account in Toronto: where the gates are
gates: Dhaka: cash into a bank — the BFIU cash-transaction report (BDT 1m, U) and the bank’s source-of-funds questions; then FERA 1947 ss.4–5: no purchase of foreign exchange or payment to a non-resident for a capital purpose without Bangladesh Bank’s permission, which has no published route for a private art purchase abroad (V on the Act; the absence of a route is this session’s finding, S).

The sale room (London, New York, Geneva): the house’s KYC and beneficial-owner declaration; in the UK the AMP’s HMRC registration and OFSI reporting duty (V); in the US the bank’s SAR and Form 8300 (V); third-party payments refused (U).
Geneva freeport: the inventory with the owner’s name and address, the tenant list, the six-month limit for export goods and customs inspection (V on the Federal Audit Office; Artnet S).

Toronto: the receiving bank’s FINTRAC EFT report at C$10,000 naming sender and beneficiary within 5 business days, the bank’s KYC and suspicious-transaction report; the CRA sees the same data (V on FINTRAC; CRA from memory, U). The art dealer in Toronto is not a FINTRAC reporting entity (S/U).
Export from Canada later: a permit under the Cultural Property Export and Import Act only if the work is 50 years old, by a dead artist and above the Group V thresholds (V).

stages.n: From cash to a bank balance
stages.rule: United States: a bank files a Currency Transaction Report for cash over US$10,000 in a business day; any trade or business, an auction house or dealer included, files Form 8300 for cash over US$10,000 in one transaction or related transactions, and may file one voluntarily for a suspicious smaller payment; cash or monetary instruments over US$10,000 carried across the border go on a CMIR; foreign accounts over US$10,000 in aggregate go on the FBAR (all per FinCEN’s 2022 alert). Treasury’s 2022 study found most market institutions ‘will not accept cash in excess of $10,000 on an annual basis from a single customer’. United Kingdom: a trader that makes or receives cash payments of £10,000 or more in total is a High Value Dealer (physical cash only, not transfers) and must register with HMRC; since 14 May 2025 HVDs and art market participants must report to OFSI as soon as practicable any known or suspected designated person or breach, on pain of up to six months’ imprisonment and OFSI penalties of up to £1m or 50% of the funds. European Union: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 sets a uniform cap of EUR 10,000 on cash payments in the commercial trade of goods from 10 Jul 2027 (member states may keep lower caps, Greece EUR 500); dealers and brokers in cultural goods of EUR 10,000 or more, and traders and warehouse keepers in free zones and bonded warehouses for such goods, stay obliged entities. Canada: the bank files an EFT report with FINTRAC for international transfers of C$10,000 or more within 5 business days (large cash reports at C$10,000, from memory, U). Switzerland’s CHF 15,000 figure for casual customers was not opened (U).
stages.cost: No fee. The cost is disclosure: the report names the depositor and, for Form 8300, the person on whose behalf the cash is paid.
stages.time: CTR within 15 days (from memory, U); FINTRAC EFT report within 5 business days; OFSI report ‘as soon as practicable’.
flags: Cash transactions, especially large bundles of cash; large-denomination notes such as the EUR 500 note (FATF 2023, Annex A).
Sanctioned persons paying large amounts of cash, especially in currencies not typically used in the art market (FinCEN FIN-2022-Alert002).
Buyers or sellers splitting a price into smaller payments, particularly negotiating it below £10,000; requests to pay in a mix of cash and cryptoassets (OFSI 2025).
Card payments just above EUR 10,000 and cash deposits with EUR 500 notes at a dealer with unclear provenance (FATF 2023, Box 28).
Simulated gallery sales, half by transfer and half in cash, to a politically exposed buyer (FATF 2023, Box 22, Brazil); false invoices for art already sold, used to legitimise cash deposits (Box 25).

stages.n: From the bank to the sale room
stages.rule: The bank, not the house, is the regulated gate in the United States: it screens the wire against OFAC’s SDN list and files a SAR when it knows, suspects or has reason to suspect that a transaction involves illicit funds, is designed to evade the BSA, lacks a lawful purpose or facilitates sanctions evasion, with no dollar threshold and the key term FIN-2022-RUSSIALUXURY; it keeps the SAR five years and may share under s.314(b). Treasury (2022) found the houses’ AML programmes ‘purely voluntary’ and that art dealers are not BSA financial institutions; the market’s own practice (government ID, proof of address, beneficial-owner declaration, source-of-funds papers above internal thresholds, refusal of third-party payments) is carried from the terminal’s earlier research, not opened on a house page this session (U). In the UK an art market participant trading or intermediating in sales of £10,000 or more, or storing art worth £10,000 or more for a person, is registered with HMRC under the Money Laundering Regulations and reports to OFSI and, separately, to the NCA by SAR. In the EU the same EUR 10,000 duty applies (FATF paras 17–18) and from 10 Jul 2027 under Regulation 2024/1624. Dollar wires clear through New York correspondent banks and so fall under OFAC wherever the parties sit (from memory, U).
stages.cost: Bank wire fees only; the house’s costs come at the buy stage.
stages.time: SWIFT wires same day to two days (from memory, U); the house’s KYC can hold a lot’s release until the papers are complete.
flags: Shell companies, trusts or third-party intermediaries (dealers, brokers, advisers, interior designers) buying, holding or selling art for a client, especially with a sanctioned-person link (FinCEN 2022; FATF 2023).
A wire for an all-cash purchase requested from a non-US bank where the funds come from another party’s account (FinCEN 2022).

Transactions structured through multiple intermediaries that obscure the ultimate beneficiary; complex structures with family trusts in intermediary jurisdictions; family members, ex-spouses and associates acting as proxies (OFSI 2025).
A common set of banks, individuals or addresses used for luxury-goods transactions with a sanctioned-person nexus; law firms in offshore centres specialising in such clients (FinCEN 2022).
Refusal to provide KYC information; unclear source of funds or ownership history; counterparties linked to sanctioned jurisdictions (OFSI 2025).
src: https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

stages.rule: Buyer’s premium on the hammer, spring 2026 (New York schedules): Christie’s, from Sept 2025, 27% to US$1.5m, 22% from US$1.5m to US$8m, 15% above US$8m; Sotheby’s, from Feb 2026, 28% to US$2m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above (the low band rose from 27% and its ceiling from US$1m); Phillips, from autumn 2025, 29% to US$2m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above, less 1–4% for a binding written bid at or above the low estimate lodged 48 hours ahead. Sales or use tax, VAT or import VAT and duty are added where the work is delivered (see the terminal’s law files); the artist’s resale right applies on resales in the UK and EU (U, not opened). Treasury (2022): under 20% of dealer sales and about 10% of auction lots exceed US$50,000, but those lots are over 85% of auction value, the segment ‘of greatest concern’.
stages.cost: On a US$1m hammer in New York in 2026: US$270,000 (Christie’s) to US$290,000 (Phillips) of premium before tax, i.e. 27–29% of the hammer; 22% on the slice between US$1.5m or US$2m and US$8m; 15% above US$8m.
stages.time: Payment is due within a short period after the sale and the lot is released only on cleared funds and completed KYC (house practice, from memory, U).
flags: Buyers indifferent to paying well above the work’s notional value; purchases far exceeding expected value; sellers not concerned with recovering their investment; unusually high margins (FATF 2023, Annex A; FinCEN 2022).
Clients uninterested in an object’s provenance, history, style or artist; purchases by intermediaries for an unnamed principal; PEPs and their associates (FATF 2023).
A price far from market value; a sale the counterparty wants completed within days with vague answers on origin (OFSI 2025, case study 2).
Newly ‘discovered’ works attributed to prominent artists; unique archaeological pieces said to relate to existing collections but never studied (FATF 2023).
src: Grossman LLP, Spring 2026 auction season: recent changes in buyer’s premiums, 14 May 2026
stages.note: Christie’s own fee pages refused the fetch twice (bot check); the schedules rest on a law firm’s May 2026 summary. The Art Newspaper of 17 Feb 2026 on Sotheby’s change not opened.

stages.rule: Switzerland: since the 2016 revision of the customs rules, free ports and open customs warehouses must keep inventories to a minimum standard showing the owner’s name and address, keep an up-to-date list of tenants and sub-tenants, hold time-limited licences (five years for open customs warehouses, ten for free ports) and move a minimum of goods a year (200 and 5,000); goods declared for export may stay six months, extendable by customs on proper grounds; an exporter must say the goods are bound for a free port and name the buyer, who must have a registered office or home abroad. The Federal Audit Office found 30 of 109 checks in early 2018 wanting and counted 7 free ports and 194 open customs warehouses in 2018 (10 and 245 in 2014). FATF (2023, para. 41): Switzerland requires free ports to inventory goods and record owners’ names and domicile addresses, which customs examine; Singapore places customer due diligence and record-keeping on licensed storage facilities. EU: from 10 Jul 2027 warehouse keepers of cultural goods of EUR 10,000 or more in free zones and bonded warehouses are obliged entities. UK: an art market participant storing art worth £10,000 or more for a person is within the OFSI reporting duty (from 14 May 2025). Luxembourg’s freeport rules, the Geneva Freeport’s own tariff and the canton’s stake were not opened (U). Storage, insurance and appraisal fees are not published on the pages opened (U).
stages.cost: Not established on an official or operator page this session (U).
stages.time: Six months for goods declared for export in a Swiss free port, extendable; no limit for goods in ordinary bonded storage (U).
flags: Storage in free zones used for anonymous transactions or to keep property beyond law enforcement’s reach; art storage described as a ‘black box’ (FATF 2023, para. 40; Treasury 2022).

Buying, keeping or cancelling insurance to protect the value of, or to cash in on the loss or theft of, art linked to a sanctioned person, where other information suggests the art is worth little (FinCEN 2022; FATF 2023).
Art storage facilities and specialist service providers are higher-risk; designated persons’ high-value goods in the UK are ‘highly likely’ unreported (OFSI 2025).
Imported or exported items not declared to customs (FATF 2023).
src: Swiss Federal Audit Office, Follow-up of the evaluation of supervisory activities at free ports and open customs warehouses, CDF-17458, 8 Apr 2019
Artnet News, Switzerland approves stricter free-port rules from 1 Jan 2016
KPMG Germany on the EU AML Regulation, Jul 2024

stages.n: From a work to a loan
stages.rule: Sotheby’s Financial Services (page of 2 Dec 2025, modified 15 Oct 2026): loans ‘from $1 million to over $250 million’, secured on the appraised value under Sotheby’s own appraisal standards, closing in about six weeks, with the art often left in the borrower’s possession subject to insurance and security conditions or else in approved storage; ‘no credit checks, income verification, or personal financial disclosures’ beyond an eligibility check; proceeds ‘can be used for nearly any purpose’; US$12bn originated since founding; the Deloitte/ArtTactic Art & Finance Report 2025 is cited for a 2025 auction-house loan book of US$3.5–5.0bn. Market (Masterworks, Jun 2026, citing Deloitte): US$34–40bn of art-secured loans outstanding going into 2026, growing 8–12% a year from about US$8bn in 2015; lenders are the private banks (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, UBS, Goldman Sachs), the houses (Sotheby’s, book about US$1.6bn; Christie’s from about US$1m) and boutiques (Athena from about US$2m; The Fine Art Group US$1m–200m); loan-to-value capped at around 50%, typically 30–50% and 40% or less in thin markets, with haircuts to peak prices; quoted rates from 2–3% to 9% or more. Treasury (2022): lenders ‘do not have a legal obligation to collect any information on the ultimate owner of the art or the source of funds’; a bank lender is itself a BSA institution and applies its own KYC (U). The UCC-1 filing, SOFR-based pricing, term lengths and the rule that proceeds go to the borrower’s own account were not found on a page opened this session (U).
stages.cost: Interest at 2–3% to 9%+ (secondary, 2026); appraisal, insurance and storage at the borrower’s charge (U).
stages.time: About six weeks to close (Sotheby’s Financial Services).
flags: A borrower unwilling to provide identification, who repays early or repays in cash (FATF 2023, Annex A).
A loan against a forged or inflated appraisal: forged paintings valued at over EUR 200m used as collateral in Italy, detected by an expert (FATF 2023, Box 30).
Art finance used to layer transactions and hide the initial illicit source of funds (Treasury 2022).
Loan proceeds wired to a third party or to a jurisdiction unconnected to the borrower (compliance practice; not on a page opened this session, U).
src: Sotheby’s Financial Services, Art-Backed Lending 101, 2 Dec 2025 (modified 15 Oct 2026)
Masterworks Research, Art lending market size and growth: where the industry stands in 2026, 10 Jun 2026
stages.note: Deloitte’s report itself was not opened; its figures arrive through Sotheby’s and Masterworks.

stages.n: From a work back to money
stages.rule: The seller pays a commission ‘agreed at the time of consignment’ that varies by category, value and expected demand (Christie’s help page; no figure published). Taxes on the gain: United States 28% maximum federal rate on long-term gains on collectibles plus the 3.8% net investment income tax; United Kingdom CGT on chattels over £6,000; France a flat tax on sales of works of art (6.5% including CRDS) or, on election, the ordinary regime; Switzerland no tax on private capital gains; Canada 50% inclusion with the C$1,000 listed-personal-property floor. These rates are carried from memory and were not opened this session (U). The artist’s resale right is deducted on EU and UK resales (U). The proceeds go to the consignor’s own account (house practice, U).
stages.cost: Seller’s commission (unpublished, negotiated) plus the tax on the gain.
stages.time: Settlement typically 35 days after the sale, once the buyer has paid (house practice, from memory, U).
flags: A seller not concerned with recovering the original investment; a sale far above or below expected value (FATF 2023; FinCEN 2022).
Sudden transfers, including sales, of high-value assets by sanctioned persons (FinCEN 2022).
Proceeds to be paid to someone other than the consignor, or to a different country (compliance practice, U).
src: https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

stages.n: From a work to a tax deduction
stages.rule: United States (IRS Art Appraisal Services page, updated 28 Jun 2026): a qualified appraisal is required where the claimed deduction for an item or group of similar items is more than US$5,000, with Form 8283 Section B attached to the return; a Statement of Value may be requested for an item appraised at US$50,000 or more, for a user fee of US$8,400 for one to three items and US$800 for each further item; claimed values are reviewed by Art Appraisal Services and the Commissioner’s Art Advisory Panel (up to 25 unpaid experts, since 1968), which generally sees works valued above US$150,000. The related-use rule for tangible personal property and the overvaluation penalties are not on that page (U). United Kingdom (DCMS guidance): the Cultural Gifts Scheme gives individuals a tax reduction of 30% of the agreed value against income tax or CGT, spread over up to five years, and companies 20% against corporation tax, for objects the Minister finds ‘pre-eminent for its national, scientific, historic or artistic interest’, assessed by the Acceptance in Lieu Panel and administered by the Arts Council; the CGS and Acceptance in Lieu (works accepted in settlement of inheritance tax) share a £40m annual limit; the recipient may not dispose of the object without the Minister’s consent. France’s dation en paiement was not opened (U).
stages.cost: The appraisal and, if sought, the IRS Statement of Value fee (US$8,400 for up to three items).
stages.time: The IRS reviews on audit; the Acceptance in Lieu Panel recommends and the Minister decides (no time stated).
flags: Donated art valued far above the price paid or above market; claims of a deduction based on an inflated appraisal (compliance practice; FATF 2023 lists overpricing generally).
Insurance taken or cancelled on donated high-value art linked to a sanctioned person (FinCEN 2022).
A dealer who sold more than 100% of the ownership of works to several parties (FATF 2023, Box 12) — a warning for fractional and gift structures.
src: IRS, Art Appraisal Services (page updated 28 Jun 2026)
DCMS, Cultural Gifts Scheme guidance (scheme of 6 Dec 2011; page dated 27 Jan 2015)
https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

stages.n: From the proceeds to another country
stages.rule: Canada: the receiving or sending bank files an EFT report with FINTRAC for any international transfer of C$10,000 or more, or two or more in 24 hours known to share a party, within 5 business days, naming requester, beneficiary, third parties, account holders and how the funds were obtained; no permission is needed, the control is the record. United States: no exchange control; CMIR at US$10,000 for cash, FBAR for foreign accounts (FinCEN 2022). United Kingdom and EU: no exchange control; the banks’ AML duties and, for designated persons, the asset freeze apply (OFSI 2025). Bangladesh: a resident may not pay a non-resident or buy foreign exchange for a capital transaction without Bangladesh Bank’s permission (FERA 1947 ss.4–5); see law_more.json for the ten capital-control entries.
stages.cost: Bank fees; the cost is the report.
stages.time: 5 business days for the FINTRAC report.
flags: Art collector’s cross-border transfers among France, Luxembourg and Switzerland (FATF 2023, Box 27); gallery manager receiving EUR 7m through a foreign trust, only EUR 2m declared to customs (Box 24).
Dealer proceeds hidden in a foreign account (FATF 2023, Box 29).
Transfers inconsistent with the customer’s profile or to a jurisdiction with no link to the customer (bank practice; not on a page opened this session, U).
src: FINTRAC, Reporting electronic funds transfers to FINTRAC (2024)
https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

typologies.n: Over- or under-invoicing between related parties: a work imported on an invoice of US$100 though appraised at about US$8m (Banco Santos case, Treasury 2022); contemporary paintings sold at about US$30,000 each with reported prices of no more than US$2,000 (FATF 2023, Box 10).
typologies.catch: Customs valuation and the appraisal on file; the FATF indicator ‘declared value far below estimated value’; the US Form 8300 and the customs entry naming the importer; Switzerland’s inventory with the owner’s name.

typologies.n: A third party pays or an intermediary buys for an undisclosed principal: advisers and interior designers buying with their own funds for a client with no duty to disclose the end client (Treasury 2022); the Rotenberg shell companies buying through agents after their 2014 designation (Treasury 2022, citing the Senate PSI report).
typologies.catch: The house’s beneficial-owner declaration and refusal of third-party payment; the bank’s SAR and OFAC screening of the payer; the FinCEN red flag on intermediaries linked to sanctioned persons; the UK OFSI reporting duty on art market participants.
src: https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

typologies.n: A loan against an inflated or forged appraisal: forged paintings valued at over EUR 200m pledged as collateral in Italy (FATF 2023, Box 30); lenders with no legal duty to identify the ultimate owner or the source of funds (Treasury 2022).
typologies.catch: The lender’s independent appraisal and expert examination (the Italian case was detected by an expert); the bank lender’s own KYC; the FATF indicator on borrowers who refuse ID or repay early or in cash.

typologies.n: A shell-company owner in a freeport: more than 1,600 works traded through shell companies and trusts (ICIJ, cited by FATF 2023, para. 65); storage facilities as ‘black boxes’ where items sit anonymously and indefinitely (Treasury 2022).
typologies.catch: Switzerland’s 2016 inventory rule (owner’s name and address, tenant list, six-month limit for export goods, customs inspection); Singapore’s CDD duty on licensed storage; the EU’s 2027 obliged-entity status for free-zone warehouse keepers of cultural goods of EUR 10,000 or more; beneficial-ownership registers.
src: Swiss Federal Audit Office, CDF-17458, 8 Apr 2019
KPMG Germany on the EU AML Regulation, Jul 2024

typologies.n: A fractional scheme: a dealer sold ‘a total of more than 100 percent ownership in an artwork’ to several buyers, pledged works as loan collateral without the co-owners’ knowledge and gave investors fraudulent contracts, including ‘a contract that listed a stolen identity as the seller’ (Inigo Philbrick, DOJ SDNY, 23 May 2022; FATF 2023, Box 12).
typologies.catch: Title and lien searches (the UCC record of a pledge), the contract naming the true seller, the lender’s and buyer’s provenance checks; in Philbrick’s case a lender’s default notice on a US$14m loan in Oct 2019 and investors’ civil suits by Nov 2019, then the FBI Art Crime Team.
src: US Attorney SDNY, Former art dealer sentenced to 7 years for $86 million fraud scheme, 23 May 2022

typologies.n: A fictitious sale or an auction bid-up by a confederate: an accomplice buys a work consigned by the launderer using criminal funds and the launderer receives a clean transfer from the auctioneer (FATF 2023, para. 67); isolated house experts able to hide identities or manipulate estimates (para. 38); NFT wash-trading (Box 5).
typologies.catch: The house’s KYC on both consignor and buyer, the Form 8300 or bank SAR on the buyer’s funds, the FATF indicators on buyers indifferent to price and sellers indifferent to recovering their investment.

typologies.n: Art as a bribe: corrupt officials paid in high-value art rather than by transfer (FATF 2023, para. 25, Box 9); bribe proceeds spent on art for a Nigerian minister’s homes (Treasury 2022).
typologies.catch: PEP screening by the house and the bank; the FATF indicator on PEPs and associates; civil forfeiture.

roundtrip.in: 27–29% of the hammer in premium at the New York houses in 2026 (Christie’s 27% to US$1.5m from Sept 2025; Sotheby’s 28% to US$2m from Feb 2026; Phillips 29% to US$2m from autumn 2025; all 22% to US$8m and 15% above), plus sales tax, VAT or import charges where the work lands (New York City 8.875% on hammer plus premium for a work delivered there, from the terminal’s v24 law file, not re-opened, U; nil in a bonded store or a no-tax state). Worked: a US$1,000,000 hammer at Christie’s New York delivered in Manhattan costs US$1,270,000 plus US$112,713 tax = US$1,382,713, i.e. 38.3% above the hammer; in bond, 27%.
roundtrip.hold: Storage, insurance and periodic appraisal: not established on an official or operator page this session (U); the Swiss rules add no fee but a six-month limit on goods declared for export.
roundtrip.out: A negotiated seller’s commission (unpublished; 10% assumed below, U) plus the tax on any gain (US 28% federal maximum on collectibles plus 3.8% NIIT, UK CGT, France’s 6.5% flat levy, Switzerland none for private persons, Canada 50% inclusion — all from memory, U) and, in the EU and UK, the artist’s resale right (U).
roundtrip.years: At break-even there is no gain and so no tax: the work must resell at a hammer that, after a 10% seller’s commission, returns the all-in cost. Delivered in Manhattan: resale hammer of US$1,536,348, a rise of 53.6% over the original hammer, which takes 8.8 years at 5% a year, 6.3 years at 7% and 5.3 years at 8.5%. Held in bond: resale hammer of US$1,411,111, a rise of 41.1%, 7.1 years at 5%, 5.1 years at 7%, 4.2 years at 8.5%. The 8.5% is the Mei Moses ten-year art return to mid-2006 (Michael Moses, Opalesque, Jan 2007; S); the long-run Mei Moses figure, Artprice and Art Basel/UBS return series were not opened (U). Premium and tax are computed from the stated schedules; the commission and return assumptions are the terminal’s, flagged U.
src: Grossman LLP, Spring 2026 auction season: recent changes in buyer’s premiums, 14 May 2026
roundtrip.note: Sotheby’s Mei Moses page refused the fetch. The arithmetic is the terminal’s own on the cited schedules.

cases.what: More than US$4.5bn allegedly misappropriated from the Malaysian fund; part laundered through fine art (Monet, Van Gogh) bought by a shell company and ‘gifted’ to co-conspirators by gift letters.
cases.how_caught: US Department of Justice civil forfeiture (Kleptocracy Asset Recovery Initiative); the works were surrendered and sold.

cases.what: After their OFAC designation in March 2014 the brothers used shell companies and an adviser to buy tens of millions of dollars of art from the major houses and in private sales (over US$18m traced by the Senate).
cases.how_caught: Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations staff report of 29 Jul 2020, cited by Treasury (2022) and FinCEN (2022).
src: https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2022-03/FinCEN Alert Russian Elites High Value Assets_508 FINAL.pdf

cases.n: Nazem Ahmad and a UK art market participant (United Kingdom, 2019–2025)
cases.what: A UK AMP dealt in art sales with Nazem Ahmad, designated for financing Hizballah, despite knowing of the links, and failed to disclose.
cases.how_caught: Guilty plea to disclosure failings under the Terrorism Act 2000 (OFSI 2025, case study 1); the US designation of Ahmad in 2019 and the 2023 indictment are from memory (U).

cases.n: Banco Santos / Edemar Cid Ferreira (Brazil/United States)
cases.what: A work imported into the United States on an invoice valuing it at US$100 though appraised at about US$8m; art valued at US$20–30m hidden, several works missing when searched.
cases.how_caught: Brazilian and US proceedings; US customs invoice found false (Treasury 2022; FATF 2023, Box 3).

cases.what: Forged paintings valued at over EUR 200m used as loan collateral.

A London and Miami dealer sold more than 100% of the ownership of works (Basquiat’s Humidity, 1982; a 2010 Christopher Wool; a 2012 Rudolf Stingel of Picasso) to several buyers, pledged works as loan collateral without co-owners’ knowledge, inflated values with fraudulent contracts and records and invented a collector; forfeiture of US$86,672,790.
cases.how_caught: A lender declared him in default on a c.US$14m loan in mid-Oct 2019; investors sued in several jurisdictions by Nov 2019; he fled to Vanuatu, was arrested there on 11 Jun 2020 by the FBI Art Crime Team, pleaded guilty and was sentenced on 23 May 2022 to 84 months and two years’ supervised release (SDNY Money Laundering and Transnational Criminal Enterprises Unit).
src: US Attorney SDNY, Former art dealer sentenced to 7 years for $86 million fraud scheme, 23 May 2022

cases.what: About US$144m of corruption proceeds laundered through art and luxury purchases (FATF 2023, Box 17); more than 2,200 artworks worth over US$15m bought with biodiesel-credit fraud proceeds (Box 20, 2013); bribe proceeds spent on art for the homes of a Nigerian oil minister (Treasury 2022).
cases.how_caught: Civil forfeiture complaints by the US Department of Justice.

cases.n: Operation Harmakis (Spain, 2016) and the Libyan antiquities
cases.what: A network trading Libyan antiquities looted by ISIL-linked groups through shell companies with false invoices describing them as decorative objects.

unconfirmed: Christie’s own premium schedule (site refused twice); the Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips schedules rest on a law firm’s May 2026 summary; The Art Newspaper of 17 Feb 2026 on Sotheby’s not opened.
Capital gains rates at the sell stage (US 28% collectibles, UK CGT, France 6.5%, Switzerland nil, Canada 50% inclusion) and the resale right: from memory, no tax-authority page opened.

Long-run art return: Sotheby’s Mei Moses page refused; only a 2007 interview (10-year return 8.5%) was read; Artprice and Art Basel/UBS return series not opened. The break-even years are the terminal’s own arithmetic on stated schedules with an assumed 10% seller’s commission.

House KYC practice (ID, proof of address, beneficial owner, source of funds, third-party payments refused, payment and settlement timing) carried from the terminal’s earlier research, not opened on a house page.
Storage, insurance and appraisal fees per year, the Geneva Freeport’s own rules and tariff, Luxembourg and Singapore freeport pages: not opened.

Art-lending terms: Sotheby’s Financial Services page gives sizes and closing time but no LTV or rate; LTV (30–50%) and rates (2–9%+) are from a June 2026 secondary citing Deloitte; UCC-1 filing, SOFR pricing and the own-account rule for proceeds not found on a page opened.

The FinCEN alert read is FIN-2022-Alert002 (16 Mar 2022); the terminal’s v24 file calls it Alert003 — the PDF opened this session says 002.
